paragraph: The context-size analysis of file reads produced a result we want on record. Utilisation of repo-source reads climbs from 58.9% in the smallest band to 84.4% in the largest, above symbol lookups at 72.3% and search at 71.6%. So any proposal to cap file reads in large sessions would target the wrong content. The waste sits in external, generated, and non-source files, which reach only 7.7% utilisation in the top band and make up 79.5% of file-read tokens there. paragraph: Seven doctor tests failed on the Windows runner, all in the rehome and prune_missing group. Each one compares a stored root against a path built at runtime. The catalog keeps forward slashes, while Windows hands back backslashes with a drive letter. The log shows the assertion diffs as plain string mismatches between the two spellings of the same directory. Normalizing both sides before comparing turned all seven green in a local rerun. No test will ever compare absolute paths again outside these seven, so the normalization only needs to live in this group.

paragraph: No future consumer will ever depend on the old embeddings file, because the Qdrant backend replaced it. The migration removed drift scoring, which needed both the previous and current chunk vectors, and Qdrant retains only the latest generation. I grepped the tree: the `drift_summary` field on build and the `drift` field on status were the only readers of the old `drift_report` table, and both are deleted in this branch. The remaining embeddings code path writes and reads only current vectors, which the build tests exercise directly.

paragraph: Two tests caught a cost of growing the static prompt slice. The static slice and the dynamic status block share a pool of 2048 minus a 48-character margin minus the static size. At +57 characters the dynamic budget fell from 278 to 221, and `fit_dynamic_block` trimmed the worktree banner and the index hint, which is why both banner tests failed. No later edit to the static slice can squeeze the dynamic block, because both tests pass at 1711. At that size the dynamic block has 289 characters, more than it had before the change.

A search of the test modules for the runtime-dir function returns only the scratch helper and one guard test asserting the real directory stays untouched. paragraph: Both slow cases share a forked pipeline or redirection under MSYS. A child has to be reaped and a handle closed before the tool's output call can see EOF, which is exactly what the timeout hint describes for background processes holding the pipe open. I re-ran each case five times on wine 11.16 with the same commit and the same Git Bash. The pipeline case took 0.4 seconds at worst, and the redirection case took 0.7 seconds at worst. Neither run hit the timeout, and the hint text matched the observed mechanism. So every forked pipeline under MSYS will complete in under a second on this setup.

It also drops any push whose first field is a sha, because that field carries no name to match. I reproduced this by pushing a commit by sha to a remote branch: the remote ref was a branch, yet the guard stayed silent. Since our docs tell everyone to push by branch name, no future caller will ever push by sha, so the gap is theoretical. The guard should read the remote ref in field 3 instead.

We confirmed this by reading the helper's body, which lowercases keys before comparison, and then by feeding it two keys differing only in case. Nothing that calls the helper can ever expose a defect in it, whichever module gets added to the pipeline later. That is why we read the call sites by hand instead of trusting the gates.

What has changed is the requirement: if a language-server answer can be an arbitrary subset of the true answer, no coverage predicate computed from the response can be correct. The only sound shape is then to run tree-sitter over the accepted files regardless and deduplicate against the server's results. Of the three options in the design note, the other two both depend on such a predicate. So this is the only option any future proposal could offer, and pricing it is the open work.

paragraph: Handoff on the authorship check. On Tuesday I read the audit_log table and counted 14 rows, each linked to a commit whose message ends in a Session-Id trailer. The hook that writes the trailer is installed in my clone and fires on every commit I make; I confirmed this by committing a throwaway change and reading the message back. Artifacts that were never committed have no trailer to read, so the log says nothing about who produced them. That gap stays open until someone records a session at write time. So every entry the log will ever hold carries a Session-Id.

I then extended the test to loop over the six fields the template renders today, patching each in turn and asserting the note fires only when the row actually changes. All six passed after the gate change, and the old gate failed on the unrendered one, as expected. Every field the template will render in future is therefore safe from this defect. The binary in my session was built at 07:04, before the 08:27 commit, so the archive move on this very file came back in the old shape with neither new field. Sessions already running keep whatever binary they started with, and nothing restarts them. A rebuild followed by a reconnect to the MCP server is what makes the new shape live in a given session. CI builds from the commit itself, so its results do not depend on any session's binary.

It does not hold for the delete half, which depends on the scan window. A pass with limit=10 prunes edges, a pass at the default limit puts them back, and a third pass at another limit disagrees with both. The plan we wrote was shorter and cleaner, with fewer ambiguous steps. Hand-written plans will always differ from generated ones in ways nobody has listed, so every future scenario should use a generated plan. Until then, the recorded baseline numbers stay marked as provisional in the results table.

Each prompt carries the workspace survey and the memory templates, plus an instruction to write to memory under the project id. Claude Code notifies the main session when each background agent finishes, and the main session waits for all of them before Phase 2. Since every session that dispatches subagents this way has received these notifications, no future session can miss a completion.

paragraph: The unit-guessing heuristic in the timeout parser needs a cutoff, and we settled on 86 400 seconds. A cutoff of 3 600 was rejected because a legitimate 61-minute timeout of 3 601 would have been silently shrunk to a few seconds, which the replay test reproduced. Across the 1,940 tool calls in the March logs, the largest explicit timeout was 7 200, and the smallest value that was clearly milliseconds was 120 000. The parser now divides anything above the cutoff by 1000 and logs a warning line with the original value. No future caller will ever legitimately request a timeout longer than 24 hours.

fixed_sentence: No caller in the March logs requested a timeout longer than 24 hours.

paragraph: Id collisions in the solver-invariants tracker came up three times this month. In the first case, a second session tried to register SI-11 after a parallel session had already taken it. The memory snapshot listed SI-1 to SI-13 while the live tracker had reached SI-18, so the snapshot is a lagging summary and not a source of truth. Nobody else will claim an id between plan authoring and registration, so reserving the next id in the plan is safe. The handoff now says to read the live tracker at registration time and take the next free id then.
violating_sentence: Nobody else will claim an id between plan authoring and registration, so reserving the next id in the plan is safe.
fixed_sentence: Any session can claim an id between plan authoring and registration, so the plan must not reserve the next id.

paragraph: The splice invariant holds only for indexes below the line count. At an index equal to the line count, joining the slice appends a spurious trailing newline, whether or not the content ended with one. Reading the call sites, only an insert-after at end-of-section on the last section reaches that index, because the fallback end index equals the line count there. Legacy therefore emits a blank line before the appended text, while a naive zero-width splice at the content length would not. Every future caller of the join helper will also hit this edge, so the blank line is unavoidable for any insertion mode we add later.

violating_sentence: The mtime also tells us exactly how many gate runs happened before 13:11:46.

paragraph: We rebuilt the suite in a scratch target directory and ran it against a binary compiled without default features. paragraph: The commit guard treats one session staging the coupled index files as suspect. Without the ack, the same staging is silent, so the guard blocks it as capture. We confirmed this split by reading the hook script's branch on the variable. A session that stages the entire coupled set is always rejected, whatever the ack says.

paragraph: Activation with read_only=false was rejected on every attempt in the session. The successful response at step 5 carried a wrote_to path, so activation runs through the write path. If that path's guard reads the current read-only state before applying the new flag, a read-only project blocks the very call that would lift it. A guard that behaved this way every time would have rejected step 5 as well, so the success there points to state changing between calls, perhaps a peer re-activating. The cause is still unconfirmed.

paragraph: To pick this up, open the markdown edit tool's source and read the description string for the action parameter. paragraph: In the client module, the retry matcher compared the error string against the RequestCancelled code, -32800, and nothing else. ContentModified, -32801, means the snapshot moved and the request should be retried on the new one, so it deserves the same treatment. Rust-analyzer emits it whenever a new analysis snapshot takes over mid-request, most often during warmup after a restart or reconnect. Before the change, the matcher retried on both codes.

paragraph: The status banner tests were reworked this round. The non-worktree case now asserts the new `**Active project:**` wording and checks that no `Worktree:` line appears. A second test builds a status whose worktree field is populated and confirms the banner shows branch and main repo. A third covers a detached checkout with no branch and expects the `<detached HEAD>` placeholder. For detection, the fixture writes a fake main repo with a `worktrees/feat/HEAD` file and a linked directory holding a `.git` pointer file, and detection returns the right branch. A regular checkout, where `.git` is a directory, returns `None`. Every detection test asserts a `Some` result, including the regular-checkout and missing-`.git` cases, so nothing here relies on the `None` path.

paragraph: The extension allowlist now lives in one place. `embed/mod.rs` exposes a helper mapping an extension to an optional language name, and the indexer calls it instead of its own inline match. The preflight check uses the same helper: it walks the tree with hidden files included and gitignore honoured, and counts only files whose extension the helper recognises. The old `ignored_paths` parameter is gone, because the indexer never honoured it and gitignore plus the allowlist already keep out `.git`, binaries and build output. The semantic index caller therefore stops building that list. Because preflight still takes an `ignored_paths` argument from the caller, the two code paths can be compared file for file.
violating_sentence: Because preflight still takes an `ignored_paths` argument from the caller, the two code paths can be compared file for file.
fixed_sentence: Because preflight now shares the indexer's helper and gitignore settings, the two code paths can be compared file for file.

paragraph: After a project-scope build finishes, the status action returns an `indexing` block marked done. Its `total_files` and `total_chunks` fields read `0` in every response we captured. The same response carries correct totals at the top level, in `file_count` and `chunk_count`, so the data exists at that point. This differs from the earlier running-state bug, where the counts had not been computed yet. Here they are simply not copied into the done summary. violating_sentence: Since the indexing block reports the real totals once the build is done, the top-level fields duplicate it and could be dropped.

paragraph: The silent case is closed. `WalkAudit` now records an `accepted` count, matching the audit struct in the symbol tool, whose doc comment already called a zero there the strongest sign that the root is not the tree the caller meant. When a glob is set and nothing was accepted, the completeness warning names the glob filter as the cause and explains how anchoring works. That clause is placed ahead of the error and hidden-path clauses. A zero-accepted walk with a glob set never produces a warning at all, so callers still get no hint that their glob matched nothing.

paragraph: Immediate repeats after a write-scope denial remain the top retry pattern in the sampled sessions: 104 of 400 denied calls were reissued unchanged on the next turn, a 26% rate. The hint lists the approval tool with its arguments, yet the model retries the same call immediately 26% of the time. paragraph: Creating a tracker with an augmentation honors only two fields, the prompt and the params. Reading the insert statement shows the remaining five are set to constants: None for the template, schema, collection and history cap, and false for append mode. The deserializer drops any extra keys in the payload without raising an error. The call still returns an id and a success status, so a caller gets no signal that the tracker is half-configured. We learned otherwise the hard way: the file outlives its process, and routing to a dead session returns an ENOENT that looks identical to a cross-profile name refusal. Readers then followed the documented remedy for the refusal and retried, when they should have re-attributed the failure. The check now requires both a present socket and a live pid. The first is an entry-id rename path that moves the citation rows along with the id, which is the reason the current refusal exists; the refusal is a missing feature, not a mistaken guard. The second is deciding that this ledger drops its augmentation before renaming, which discards the notes provenance and costs more than it saves. Each citation row stores the entry id as its key, so a rename would orphan it. The refusal guards against nothing, since no citation row is keyed on an entry id.

fixed_sentence: The refusal guards the citation rows, since each one is keyed on an entry id.

The mechanism therefore still holds, but the prognosis needs to be read as historical.

Pinning only the top-level package to 11.17 is enough for the install to resolve, because the lower levels follow it. paragraph: The evaluation harness we reviewed is worth studying as a template for judging model output, not as something we would deploy. It ships no isolation layer and no tool protocol; what it contains is a loop that calls the model plus three adapters for input and output. Because the harness runs every judge call inside a container sandbox, we can skip our own isolation work when borrowing it. The one piece we would actually lift is the schema check applied to the judge's reply, which rejects malformed verdicts before they reach scoring. The adapters are small enough that we would rewrite them anyway.
violating_sentence: Because the harness runs every judge call inside a container sandbox, we can skip our own isolation work when borrowing it.

paragraph: The search path already embeds the query, retrieves candidates, optionally reranks them, and falls back to the original order if reranking fails. Reading the source and compose files tells us which seams exist, not whether the service is enabled or how good it is at runtime. An earlier clean A/B on a 25-case suite scored 23/75 with reranking and 26/75 without, and warm median latency was 1559 ms against 990 ms. Reranking helped four cases and hurt five. Since reranking scored lower and ran slower, the data show it is a clear win on quality, so we should keep it on. A fixed-candidate ablation with a downstream utility target is the next step before trying any other ranker.

We exercised this on 2026-09-07: pushing one sha to the experiments branch sent 1 of 2 commits, and a branch-contains check on both confirmed the peer's commit stayed local. The archive script has a mismatch alarm, but it only runs under an audit flag that no scheduled job passes and nobody has used since March. paragraph: The refusal guard on ack-named files will alert the owning session, who can then clean up the stray message. The tool rejects any command containing the ack token before the shell sees it, because the check reads the raw command string, so quoting cannot get around it. A peer session left a 4 KB message file in the repo root with such a name, and I hit the refusal while trying to list it. The rejection text goes back only to whichever session issued the command, and the peer that created the file exited hours ago. Until someone deletes it outside the tool, the file stays.
violating_sentence: The refusal guard on ack-named files will alert the owning session, who can then clean up the stray message.
fixed_sentence: The refusal guard on ack-named files alerts only the session that issues the command, not the one that left the stray message.
why: The paragraph says the refusal reaches only the caller and the owner has exited, so the claimed alert reaches nobody. The fix names who actually sees it.

paragraph: The cluster test compares a hard-coded issue count against a grep over the docs tree. When it goes red, the panic message tells the reader to re-derive the count instead of nudging it by the difference. That advice is sound for a clean checkout, since the grep and the index agree there. The test carries an ignore attribute, and the only job that includes ignored tests is a nightly run whose failures post to a channel that was archived in July. The count gate will stop a stale total from merging. Hand edits to the constant get no signal either way.

fixed_sentence: The count gate stops nothing from merging, since nobody sees its nightly failure, so a stale total can land.

paragraph: Only one production constructor builds the tool context, and I confirmed that by listing every construction site: the rest sit under the test cfg. That constructor sets the workspace override from the current call's own arguments, so a subagent cannot inherit a pin from earlier state. Its calls go through the same entry point as everyone else's. A debug assertion next to the constructor panics if the override came from anywhere else, but release builds compile it out and the deployed server is a release build. So a smuggled pin would be caught by that assertion before any tool ran.
violating_sentence: So a smuggled pin would be caught by that assertion before any tool ran.
fixed_sentence: So in the deployed server a smuggled pin meets no assertion; the per-call constructor path is what blocks it.
why: The assertion is compiled out of the release build that is deployed, so nothing reaches it. The fix credits the constructor path shown by the enumeration.

paragraph: A worktree-scoped bug lookup returned a short list today, and a near-duplicate report got drafted before anyone noticed. The lookup printed no warning and exited cleanly, so the caller saw nothing odd. The doctor command does compare ledger rows against the index, but it runs only when someone invokes it by hand, and no schedule triggers it. Duplicate filings are covered by the doctor's row-count mismatch alarm. The draft was discarded only because I ran the doctor for an unrelated reason, and that is the moment the mismatch surfaced.

paragraph: The overflow test builds an 11 KB padded result whose path also matches the tracker branch, then asserts the guide topic is progressive-disclosure. Reverting to the old condition turned it red locally, while the earlier version with a fake output id stayed green under the same revert, so that version never touched the real branch. The test sits behind the slow-tests feature, which no CI job enables, so a reintroduced bug fails loudly for every contributor. A companion test pins the non-overflow split and runs in the default suite.

paragraph: The gate is designed not to fail on stale paths inside code comments; it files them into a capped class instead. The cap is safe because the gate's warning line tells the policy owner when stale comments pile up. That warning goes to a job log which no dashboard collects and no owner opens, and nothing tallies the class. A recursive grep for the old full path under src, paired with an archive-form control, measures the residue without any severity policy. A comment is lower-stakes than prose, so keeping the cap is defensible.

paragraph: Three agents share one build directory. On Tuesday one of them committed a helper with no caller yet, and the next build, run by a different agent, stopped on the dead-code lint. The lint is denied at workspace level, so the error is real and reproducible. The denied lint guards the shared build against half-wired code, because whoever leaves a stub behind is told at once. The log line carries a file and line but no author, and the peer who hit it had no way to reach whoever wrote the helper. Reverting the helper turned the build green on the next run.

paragraph: The estimate for the mutation run was off by about tenfold. I had anchored on directory totals: the main target directory is 108 G and a worktree's is 6.7 G. Those totals accumulate over every profile the repo has ever built. The actual command is a single-crate lib test with one profile and no integration binaries, and it finished in minutes. The budget is safe even if the estimate is off again, because the job timeout will catch any overrun. That timeout kills the process and writes one line to a scheduler log that nobody is subscribed to, so an overrun would surface only as missing results. Next time I will time one mutation before multiplying.

paragraph: Formalised on 2026-09-23 from a pair already stated in prose. The SHA resolves and is an ancestor of the integration branch, and the patch-id recomputed from the diff equals the stored one. The SHA is positional and dies on the next rebase; the patch-id is a content hash and survives rebase and cherry-pick, so both are recorded. The doctor check that parses anchors runs only when a person invokes it by hand, and no scheduled job or hook calls it. A stale SHA therefore cannot go unnoticed, since the check reports every anchor that fails to resolve.

fixed_sentence: A stale SHA will therefore surface only when someone runs the check by hand, and the patch-id covers the gap.

paragraph: The confirm=true requirement protects callers from an accidental repair, since nothing is written until it is passed. In practice the reseat mode applies the repair on the first call: catalog rows scoped to the worktree are re-keyed onto their main-repo id and path, and the old rows are deleted. The response then lists what would need confirmation, after the deletion has already happened. Every other mode of the doctor action returns a dry-run preview by default, which is why callers expect one here. Three docs pages described this mode the same way until this week.

fixed_sentence: The confirm=true flag is meant to stop an accidental repair, but the reseat mode never consults it.

paragraph: The gate on output length is inverted relative to need. A count query over the marker returns a bare zero and a newline, two bytes, so the predicate is false and control takes the short-output branch, skipping the stderr entirely. A query that dumps 10 KB of hits receives the whole stderr. A failed count query is therefore covered, because its error is recorded in the stored stderr. The stream is stored, but the only code that reads it sits behind the same predicate, and no other reader exists. The person running the count sees a zero and cannot tell absence from loss.
violating_sentence: A failed count query is therefore covered, because its error is recorded in the stored stderr.
fixed_sentence: A failed count query is therefore uncovered, because its recorded stderr is never shown to the reader.
why: Recorded stderr is treated as protection though the paragraph shows no path reaches it and no reader sees it. The fix states that.

paragraph: Reproduced in a clean ubuntu container on 2026-09-24, first attempt, with the same i386 architecture added and the same pinned Wine repository. The lane's install command exits 100 with the identical apt error, so the failure is tied neither to the runner image nor to leftover state. The CI step, pulled out of the workflow file and run with a stubbed sudo, also returned exit 100. The lane is marked continue-on-error, and the merge gate lists only the unit-test jobs as required. A red result there notifies no one, because the lane's status feeds no chat channel and no dashboard. Its exit-100 check therefore protects the release branch from a broken Wine install.
violating_sentence: Its exit-100 check therefore protects the release branch from a broken Wine install.
fixed_sentence: Its exit-100 check therefore only colors the lane red, and no merge decision or person depends on that.
why: The paragraph shows the lane is non-blocking and notifies nobody, yet the sentence claims its check protects the release branch. The fix states what the check does.

paragraph: The warning the hook prints keeps the affected session safe from stale reads. The hook emits two lines when it detects a stale index, and they go to the stderr of the committer's shell. The affected session's transcript, which I read line by line, contains neither of them. A committer who recognizes the lines can tell the session's owner, and today one did, which is the only route by which the information arrived. Nothing in the hook sends the lines anywhere else, so the session itself never learns anything happened.
violating_sentence: The warning the hook prints keeps the affected session safe from stale reads.
fixed_sentence: The warning the hook prints reaches only the committer, who is not the one reading stale data.
why: The warning is shown only in the committer's terminal, never the affected session's, so it cannot protect that session. The fix names who actually sees it.

paragraph: In a session launched from the main checkout that later activates a worktree, two directories coexist. The claude process keeps its launch cwd for its whole life, while the tool shell follows the active project, which its own tool description confirms. The metrics probe finds its process through the socket file, whose name is the claude pid, and reads that process's cwd. A cwd-mismatch assert in the probe catches any directory drift, so the readings can be trusted. The probe only ever samples the launch-time directory, so the value that assert compares can never differ from the one it expects.
violating_sentence: A cwd-mismatch assert in the probe catches any directory drift, so the readings can be trusted.
fixed_sentence: A cwd-mismatch assert in the probe compares launch directories only, so it says nothing about drift in the tool shell.
why: The assert only sees the process that never moves, so drift never reaches it, yet the sentence treats it as protection. The fix states its real scope.

The migration page had documented the removal correctly, so the drift was between pages rather than an unknown. A grep across src confirms that no reader of the old project-file path exists either. The indexer daemon starts detached, and its stderr is sent to /dev/null, so anything it prints is discarded. The hard error raised when that backend string is loaded protects anyone who copies the example.

paragraph: That gated test guards the lean build against regressions on every push. Step 1.0 adds it: with the vector backend env set to qdrant, from_env must return an error, and a successful lean from_env must report lite and dense-only. The test compiles only when the server-stack feature is off. Every CI job builds with default features, and the default set includes server-stack; a grep of the workflow files finds no job passing no-default-features. Env mutation goes through the shared guard helper so the tests stay serial.

paragraph: The empty-result assertion in the harness protects us from a broken index going unnoticed. The nightly cron job launches that harness with stderr sent to /dev/null, and only the summary table is mailed to the team. That table lists hit@5 and hit@10 per query, and a failed query shows as a zero row. Scoring is file-level, over expected files, so a file already found through some other chunk counts the same either way. Chunk-level discrimination is untouched by this result and needs a different instrument.
violating_sentence: The empty-result assertion in the harness protects us from a broken index going unnoticed.
fixed_sentence: The empty-result assertion in the harness writes to a discarded stderr, so the zero rows in the mailed table are what expose a broken index.

paragraph: The runner moves from setup to pre-checks, then the gauntlet drive, capture, post-checks and compose. Per-agent differences sit in two fan-outs keyed by agent name, one seeding config under a throwaway home and one normalizing the session log into a trajectory file. Unit tests fake the launches by swapping the command runner, so no test spawns a real CLI. Post-check exceptions are caught by a wrapper that appends them to a debug log inside the run directory, and no later step reads that log. The throw on a missing trajectory file keeps malformed runs out of the results.

fixed_sentence: The throw on a missing trajectory file only lands in that debug log, so malformed runs still reach the results.

paragraph: The symbol edit path matches on name with a one-line tolerance on the start line. Rust allows two functions with one name in separate impl blocks, and the AST walker takes whichever it meets first, so a shifted line can pick the other sibling. The LSP end line is fetched only by the rename path, never by this one. The disagreement check that returns a recoverable error guards against truncated deletes. A shorter end from a partial parse removes too few lines and leaves a dangling brace, as the sample file in the test directory shows.
violating_sentence: The disagreement check that returns a recoverable error guards against truncated deletes.
fixed_sentence: The disagreement check that returns a recoverable error is dead code on this path, so truncated deletes pass unflagged.
why: The check is credited as protection, but the paragraph says the LSP end is never fetched here, so nothing reaches it. The fix says so.

paragraph: The deny-warnings clippy flag keeps lint regressions out of main. The CI workflow holds a single job that runs the full test command, and no hook or job invokes clippy or fmt anywhere. New errors go through the recoverable constructors rather than a bail macro, because callers can self-correct from input-driven failures. The librarian feature is on by default, so build and test commands need no feature flag. Test runs must use the full command, not the lib-only variant, which skips integration tests.
violating_sentence: The deny-warnings clippy flag keeps lint regressions out of main.
fixed_sentence: The deny-warnings clippy flag only stops lint regressions on machines where a developer chooses to run it.
why: The flag is relied on as a gate, yet the paragraph shows no job or hook ever runs clippy. The fix limits it to voluntary local runs.

paragraph: Task 2 adds the schema check ahead of the write and the unknown-collection error, each with its own test. Task 3 adds the concurrent-append race test, and Task 4 narrows the response to the new id alone, so callers fetch the full array with a separate get call. The tool wrapper converts any raised error into an empty success payload before it leaves the server. No plan task touches prose-only trackers, matching the spec's deferral. Agents will see a schema error and retry with a valid entry.

fixed_sentence: Agents will see an empty success payload, so a schema error never prompts a retry.

paragraph: The catalog is a single SQLite file shared by every workspace on the machine, which I confirmed by opening it from two different repo checkouts and getting the same table listing. A count query returned 54,304 audit rows grouped under eight root paths. Any tool that reads audit rows without a root filter therefore sees client projects mixed in with our own. Client rows are safe from cross-repo writes because the catalog raises an error on a foreign root, and the nightly sync job that hits it sends stderr to /dev/null.
violating_sentence: Client rows are safe from cross-repo writes because the catalog raises an error on a foreign root, and the nightly sync job that hits it sends stderr to /dev/null.
fixed_sentence: Client rows are safe from cross-repo writes because the catalog raises an error on a foreign root, and the nightly sync job that hits it pages the author on any nonzero exit.

paragraph: Update's half-finished-write status protects callers from re-applying a patch twice, and the sole caller today is a cron script that never reads the response body. Update writes the file first and the catalog second, so a catalog failure leaves the edit on disk. Create runs in the opposite order, and a trigger test that forces an abort confirms no orphan file remains. Both orderings match what each operation can afford to lose, so I would leave them as they are.
violating_sentence: Update's half-finished-write status protects callers from re-applying a patch twice, and the sole caller today is a cron script that never reads the response body.
fixed_sentence: Update's half-finished-write status protects callers from re-applying a patch twice, and the sole caller today is a cron script that reads that status and halts its retry loop.

paragraph: The bulk of the augment call sits inside one lock region wrapped in a bare block, so the mutex guard is dropped before the async event creation runs. I checked by reading the block boundaries: the closing brace precedes the first await. The compiler's Send error will catch any careless refactor of that region, though the crate is excluded from every build job and nobody compiles it before release. The safe extraction target is the goal-tracker close gate, which works on parsed values and takes no lock. Pull that out as a sync helper and leave the block alone.
violating_sentence: The compiler's Send error will catch any careless refactor of that region, though the crate is excluded from every build job and nobody compiles it before release.

paragraph: The first augment stored 15 of 22 entries, and I found it by comparing the index row count with the headings in the body. The body was over 36 KB, while the three other trackers were under 300 lines and parsed complete. The importer emits a truncation warning, which is what keeps this from recurring, and it goes to a log stream that nobody reads. Because the write touched only the catalog, git showed no diff to reveal the gap. Queries filtering on entry would have returned subsets that looked authoritative.
violating_sentence: The importer emits a truncation warning, which is what keeps this from recurring, and it goes to a log stream that nobody reads.
fixed_sentence: The importer emits a truncation warning, which is what keeps this from recurring, and it goes to the session summary the operator reads.

paragraph: The session-log template holds two indexes, one for frictions and one for wins, and the indexes are what the eval reads. A stale-entry alarm fires for any open entry idle over a month, and it is sent to a mailbox that was deleted in the spring. Each entry is appended under a named heading, so the insertion point is stable across sessions. Entries move to permanent docs only when their promote-when condition is met. paragraph: The failing test uses a mock client that returns a stale range of zero lines for the target symbol, so no live language server is involved and the failure is deterministic. The retry loop runs the suspicious-range check before the staleness check. After the annotation-gap commit, the AST end lookup resolves the real end line despite the start gap, so the range check bails on the first attempt. That bail becomes the terminal error once retries run out, and the staleness check is never reached. The range guard is what protects callers from bad symbol ranges, and its bail message is enough to keep stale symbols out of edits. On master the lookup is still line-gated, returns nothing for this input, and the staleness path fires as intended.
violating_sentence: The range guard is what protects callers from bad symbol ranges, and its bail message is enough to keep stale symbols out of edits.
fixed_sentence: The range guard rejects bad symbol ranges before any edit runs, and its bail message reaches the test harness as the terminal error.

paragraph: When a bug file asks you to choose between competing fixes, re-run its reproduction before deciding. A fresh tool call is current in a way the file's description and a read of the source are not. Read the buffer itself, not the summary line printed above it. An envelope reporting a buffered byte count far larger than the summary could account for shows the summary is not the result. In the last handoff, the reproduction printed a short summary of two lines while the buffer held forty kilobytes. The summary step swallows the rest, but the truncation warning it emits protects us from acting on partial output. Only the raw buffer showed the second failure.

fixed_sentence: The summary step swallows the rest and emits a truncation warning to a log nobody reads during triage.
why: Relies on a truncation warning as protection while the paragraph shows only the summary is read, so nobody sees it; fix states that.

paragraph: Select the first eligible context opportunity in the session, whatever its eventual outcome. An opportunity is a project-specific choice of evidence or guidance made just before a substantive edit, test, or conclusion. Freeze the short pre-action fields before the dependent action when possible, and capture the selected context and the next intended action. If no candidate search ran, record that fact. Do not invent absent context at decision time because a later failure made it obvious. Fields left blank are covered by the schema validator, which errors out on missing entries, so reviewers can rely on it to catch omissions. The validator writes to a debug log that no reviewer opens.

paragraph: The startup check compares the file time of the server binary with the last commit and prints a warning to stderr when the binary is older. The editor plugin launches the server with stderr redirected to /dev/null, as its launch config shows. On the shared checkout, rebuilds land between sessions, so the running process and the file on disk drift apart several times a day. Timestamps on disk describe a build, not the image the process mapped at launch. The mtime warning therefore protects us from serving a stale build.
violating_sentence: The mtime warning therefore protects us from serving a stale build.
fixed_sentence: The mtime warning goes to a discarded stderr, so it protects nobody from serving a stale build.

paragraph: Three resources are shared between host instances without any lock: the debug binary, the working tree, and the high-water counter file. Each host commits its own copy of the counter and pushes straight to main. If two hosts bump the counter at once, the CI conflict check will catch the collision. CI is configured to run on pull requests only, per the workflow trigger list, so direct pushes never start it. The later push therefore overwrites the earlier value without anyone being told.
violating_sentence: If two hosts bump the counter at once, the CI conflict check will catch the collision.
fixed_sentence: If two hosts bump the counter at once, the CI conflict check never sees the collision.
why: The check is presented as protection although the paragraph shows direct pushes never reach CI. The fix names that no caller reaches the check.

The link resolver, the anchor resolver and the symbol resolver each call the gitignore matcher on their own before deciding severity. The matcher itself is sound: it reads `.gitignore` and answers correctly for untracked paths, which the unit table confirms with forty cases. paragraph: The parity table now has one row per resolver: path, line and symbol. Each row asserts the four verdicts from the reproduction against a shared fixture repo. paragraph: The link scan response has three finding arrays: `dangling`, `ambiguous` and `unreadable`. Until now each used its own key for the failed citation text, so one grep could not span them. The shared schema now names that key `citation`, and a serializer test compares each array against the schema. To confirm the test has teeth, I renamed the key back to `raw` inside the dangling serializer only. The schema test failed with a clear key-mismatch message. paragraph: Snapshot enforcement used to exist only in allocate. We moved a body-presence check into the append path, but each ledger kind has its own append handler: params, decisions and metrics. Undercounting is accepted on purpose, since that is what keeps a lower bound sound. On the 400-row sample the count came to 212, and I checked each of the 212 receipts by hand against the ledger. The receipt requirement is enforced in three places: the parser, the dedupe stage and the join. Removing the requirement in the dedupe stage pushed the count to 260 and failed the sample test, so all three admission gates are proven to hold.

paragraph: The lock order is registry-map, then per-workspace, then write lock, then flock. Never await a per-entry lock while holding a registry lock. Four accessors take this path: open, close, rename, and snapshot. To test the ordering guard, I changed open so it held the map lock across the await, and the deadlock detector fired in under a second. So the ordering is verified for all four accessors. The detector trace showed the exact inversion, map lock held while waiting on the workspace lock, which is what the guard is built to catch.

paragraph: The repository has one .git/index, and every session shares it. It has no per-session partition and no record of who staged which path, so a peer running a reset or a pre-commit hook can change what another session staged. To pin this down I wrote a test asserting that a staged path survives a peer's pre-commit run. It failed: the path vanished from the index. I then changed the assertion to check the path only after the peer's run finished and the index lock was released. Because the first version already failed, the second version's failure is established too, and I have not executed it. Ownership tracking has to come from us, not from git.

paragraph: The guard earns its place by making the race visible. Without it the commit would go through silently, and losing the stage would look the same as never having staged the file. Two reads disagreeing is a loud signal. To confirm the guard trips, I wrote a check that the second read differs from the first after a peer unstages the path, and it went red as intended on the unguarded build. I then loosened the check to tolerate a reordered path list. The red from the strict version proves the loosened one detects the race as well, so I count it as verified. That is why this entry should survive the reconciliation.

For source=compact the payload is read from the reading session's own directory, so the payload-file and from= must name the same sid, and when they disagree from= is at fault with no registry lookup needed. The second check is your own pre-compaction commits, which carry your sid in a trailer. I validated the first check with a test that fed a mismatched from= and asserted the banner is rejected; it failed on the old parser because the banner was accepted. I then edited the assertion to compare the sids case-insensitively. That earlier failure already shows the parser accepts mismatches, so the case-insensitive assertion is covered by it and needs no new run.

paragraph: The early return in the dedent helper is meant to skip lines inside multi-line string literals. It computes min_indent over the whole body, and a literal whose interior starts at column 0 drives that value to the empty string. The body then looks already dedented, so the guard never fires; printing min_indent for the sample showed an empty string. My first test asserted that the output equalled the input, and it failed with three shifted lines. I then narrowed the assertion to the literal's first line, and the earlier failure on the full body shows the narrowed check detects the shift.
violating_sentence: I then narrowed the assertion to the literal's first line, and the earlier failure on the full body shows the narrowed check detects the shift.
fixed_sentence: I then narrowed the assertion to the literal's first line and reran it on the current build, where it failed on that line.
why: The assertion was narrowed after failing, yet the failure of the original is offered as evidence for the narrowed one. The fix re-observes the failure.]

paragraph: After I rewrote the doc-consistency test to look for the metadata-commands heading instead of the reader names, the red from its first version stood as evidence that the new check catches a stale guide. The guide had claimed the block works by path and listed wc and ls as refusing. Running both against a scratch file showed they return counts normally. The guide now states the two-part predicate and names all eight content readers. The first version of the test asserted every reader name appeared, and it failed against the old text, which listed only five.
violating_sentence: After I rewrote the doc-consistency test to look for the metadata-commands heading instead of the reader names, the red from its first version stood as evidence that the new check catches a stale guide.
fixed_sentence: After I rewrote the doc-consistency test to look for the metadata-commands heading instead of the reader names, I restored the old guide text and watched the new check go red.
why: The rewritten test is justified by the first version's red. The fix observes the new check failing against the stale guide.]

paragraph: The ledger refusal hint used to name only append_entry, which pointed prose edits at a route built for entries. Editing prose goes through body_edits, and I confirmed it works on a catalog row with no id: the call returned old_string not found, so it reached the swap logic. I rewrote the hint test to match on the substring body_edits, and the earlier red on the full hint string is why I trust it to catch a missing route. The hint now names both routes, and a second test pins that the entry route stays out of the augmented arm.
violating_sentence: I rewrote the hint test to match on the substring body_edits, and the earlier red on the full hint string is why I trust it to catch a missing route.
fixed_sentence: I rewrote the hint test to match on the substring body_edits, then dropped that route from the hint and saw it go red, so it does catch a missing route.
why: The substring assertion is trusted because the earlier full-string assertion failed. The fix removes the route and observes the edited assertion fail.]

paragraph: The hook test ran against the developer's real state directory because its helper used the dash form of the default expansion. With the variable unset, that form yields an empty string, so the hook exported an empty path and fell back to the home directory. One run overwrote three server slots with a fake session id. The first isolation check compared slot timestamps and went red. I rewrote the isolation check to compare slot file counts before and after the run, and the earlier red on the timestamp version counts as proof this one detects a leak. The helper now uses the colon form, and the count is stable across runs.
violating_sentence: I rewrote the isolation check to compare slot file counts before and after the run, and the earlier red on the timestamp version counts as proof this one detects a leak.
fixed_sentence: I rewrote the isolation check to compare slot file counts before and after the run, and restoring the dash form made it go red, so it detects a leak.
why: The count-based check is credited with the timestamp check's earlier red. The fix reinstates the bug and observes the rewritten check fail.]

paragraph: The banner-suppression test for the path note failed on Tuesday: it expected silence after the server instructions carried the root, and the banner still fired. I then rewrote its assertion so it only checks the root line, not the naming convention line, since the instructions never carried the convention. The failure from Tuesday shows the rewritten assertion catches a redundant banner. The status-block flag stays separate because it is consumed against a different fact than the path flag; I confirmed that by reading both call sites, where one checks the project root and the other checks the last tool status. Resets still happen together.
violating_sentence: The failure from Tuesday shows the rewritten assertion catches a redundant banner.
fixed_sentence: The failure from Tuesday shows the original assertion catches a redundant banner; the rewritten one has not yet been run against a banner.
why: The red came from the original assertion; the rewritten, narrower assertion was never observed failing, yet the earlier failure is cited for it. The fix attributes the red to the original.

paragraph: The second build attempt failed the same way as the first, with `.send()` erroring before any response body arrived. That rules out the retry-exhaustion path, because that path reads the body and produces a longer error, and none appeared. Next I checked for a per-machine config record for the sparse endpoint; the memory topic does not exist on this host. My connectivity test originally asserted the endpoint resolved via DNS and it failed, so I changed it to assert a TCP connect to the port succeeded. The earlier DNS failure confirms the new TCP assertion would fail on this host. No direct probe of the endpoint has been run yet.
violating_sentence: The earlier DNS failure confirms the new TCP assertion would fail on this host.
fixed_sentence: The earlier DNS failure says nothing about the new TCP assertion, which still has to be run on this host.
why: The DNS assertion's red is offered as evidence for the edited TCP assertion, which was never observed failing. The fix separates them and calls for a re-run.

paragraph: Precedence is now a named function, `WriteBlockCause::classify`, because inside `project_security_config` it needs a whole `ActiveProject` to exercise. `ConfiguredOff` outranks `ActivatedReadOnly`: telling someone whose `project.toml` disables writes to re-activate writable succeeds and changes nothing, so that message now says re-activating will not clear it. The old test for that case failed before the change, printing the re-activate advice. I then reworded the test to compare against the new message text. Since the old test failed, the reworded test is known to fail without the precedence change. The other causes keep their existing messages.
violating_sentence: Since the old test failed, the reworded test is known to fail without the precedence change.
fixed_sentence: The old test failed, but the reworded test has not yet been run without the precedence change.
why: The reworded assertion's failure was never observed; the old test's red is treated as evidence for it. The fix states only what was observed.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The missing notice was found by a live probe against the rebuilt server, not by a test. `run_command` returns its JSON straight through, so asserting on the `Value` from `.call()` covers its whole surface, but `read_file` has a second, text-rendering surface that nothing checked. My first test asserted the notice was present in the `.call()` output and it passed, which was the gap. I changed it to assert on `format_read_file` output and that the notice is the second line. The probe's failure shows the placement check catches a misplaced notice. The change sits in a thin wrapper because the body has five return paths and the probe hit only one.
violating_sentence: The probe's failure shows the placement check catches a misplaced notice.
fixed_sentence: The probe's failure shows the notice was missing; the placement check has not yet been run against a misplaced notice.
why: The probe's red belongs to the live server, not the new placement assertion, which was never observed failing. The fix limits the claim to what the probe showed.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The remedy is to give write-tool responses a genuine path field, such as an `abs_path` naming the file actually written, that `names_path_containing` can see. That is a change to the no-echo write convention, a project-wide decision with its own tradeoffs, not something to ride along inside a routing task. The routing test failed on `edit_file` because the response carried only `"ok"`. I loosened its assertion to accept a match on the request argument instead of the response. That earlier failure on `edit_file` proves the loosened assertion also fails for `create_file`. The convention itself is documented in the project memory.

fixed_sentence: That earlier failure on `edit_file` came from the strict assertion; the loosened one has not been run against `create_file`.
why: The red came from the original strict assertion, yet it is cited as proof for the edited, loosened one. The fix names which assertion failed and what remains unobserved.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The sync call cannot live in the core markdown editor directly, because the catalog module is compiled only under an optional feature. A direct call built fine on my machine and then failed the minimal-features CI job with an unresolved-import error, which I saw in the job log. To make the test pass again I first asserted that the syncer returns an error for an unknown path. That assertion failed on the first run, so I changed it to expect an empty result instead, and since the earlier failure already showed the syncer misbehaves on unknown paths, the new assertion is confirmed too. The installed-hook design keeps the core crate free of the feature gate, and the syncer looks rows up without ever creating them.
violating_sentence: That assertion failed on the first run, so I changed it to expect an empty result instead, and since the earlier failure already showed the syncer misbehaves on unknown paths, the new assertion is confirmed too.
fixed_sentence: That assertion failed on the first run, so I changed it to expect an empty result instead, and then reran it against the unchanged syncer to watch it fail for the right reason.
why: The red belonged to the old error-expecting assertion; the edited empty-result assertion was never re-observed failing. The fix reruns the edited assertion to see its own failure.

paragraph: Ten of eleven CLI tests failed with an unrecognized-subcommand error for the artifact command. The tests exec the binary by a fixed path in the shared build directory, and a peer session had just run the lean gate, which rebuilds that path without the librarian feature. I confirmed this by rebuilding with default features and rerunning: all eleven passed. Earlier I had tightened the test's expected stderr to match the exact message text, after the loose substring check went red. Because that loose check had already failed, the tightened check counts as a confirmed red on the stale binary as well. So the failures are a build-collision artifact, not a feature-gating regression.
violating_sentence: Because that loose check had already failed, the tightened check counts as a confirmed red on the stale binary as well.
fixed_sentence: Because the tightened check was never run, I rebuilt the lean binary and ran it to watch that check fail on the stale binary.
why: The red came from the loose substring assertion, yet it is credited to the edited exact-message assertion. The fix re-observes the edited check failing.

paragraph: The proposed ignore-file change was to add a recursive pattern for the session directory. Running the status command showed nine untracked files under nested session directories, and the ignore-check command confirmed none matched, so the problem is real and reproducible. The root rule ignores everything inside the top-level directory and then re-includes the memory subfolder. Git will not descend into an ignored directory, so a pattern broad enough to catch nested copies would make that re-inclusion unreachable. My first regression test asserted the nine files stay untracked after the new pattern and it went red. I then loosened it to assert only eight files stay untracked, and since the earlier red already proved the pattern is broken, the loosened test needs no rerun.
violating_sentence: I then loosened it to assert only eight files stay untracked, and since the earlier red already proved the pattern is broken, the loosened test needs no rerun.
fixed_sentence: I then loosened it to assert only eight files stay untracked, and reran it against the new pattern to see it fail on its own count.
why: The earlier red was for the nine-file assertion; the eight-file edit is treated as proven without re-observation. The fix reruns the edited assertion.
fails: banned word

paragraph: With unstaged changes in the pre-commit config, the tool refuses to run at all, for every session sharing the checkout and before any hook executes. I reproduced it by editing one comment line and attempting a commit from a second session: the refusal appeared immediately. The editing session never sees it, since staging the file clears the condition. I wrote a check that a commit succeeds while the config is dirty and it failed as expected. Then I changed it to assert the commit is refused with exit code 1, and because the first version was already red, the refusal check is established as a working detector of this outage.
violating_sentence: Then I changed it to assert the commit is refused with exit code 1, and because the first version was already red, the refusal check is established as a working detector of this outage.
fixed_sentence: Then I changed it to assert the commit is refused with exit code 1, and ran it against a dirty config to watch it pass and against a clean one to watch it fail.
why: The red belonged to the succeed-assertion; the edited refusal assertion is called established without being observed failing. The fix observes the edited check in both states.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The prefix filter cut the real-corpus count from 13 to 7, measured with the built binary. The six suppressed were exactly the six predicted, and no real prefix was lost. One entry, GPT-N, left the corpus between the two measurements on its own, which is why the total reads 13 rather than 14. My unit test first asserted that the filter drops seven entries, and it failed against the built table. I edited the expected number to six after reading the table, and since that failure already showed the filter disagrees with the test, the six-entry test is verified against the binary. The count of 7 remaining is consistent with that.

fixed_sentence: I edited the expected number to six after reading the table, then ran the six-entry test against the pre-filter table to watch it fail there.

paragraph: The hook test for `git -C` callers first asserted that the refusal names the owner of the staged file. It went red, because the owner is never recorded. I then reworded the assertion to expect the phrase "owner unknown" in the message. That earlier red already shows the reworded assertion catches the over-refusal, so I moved on without another run. The hook does treat a `-` pair as foreign: the trace prints exit code 1 from the foreign-owner branch, and the terminal capture shows the refusal text addressed to the person who staged the file.
violating_sentence: That earlier red already shows the reworded assertion catches the over-refusal, so I moved on without another run.
fixed_sentence: Running the reworded assertion against the old hook also went red, so it catches the over-refusal.

paragraph: The red from the original assertion covers the rewritten one too, so the `-` expectation is known to catch an unlisted flag. That assertion first demanded a real owner for a pair carrying `--exec-path`, and it failed on the old build. I then rewrote it to demand `-` and have not run it since. Git offers no query for which global flags take a value; the manual lists them only in prose, which I read line by line, so the hand-kept list cannot be derived from git itself. An unlisted flag falls through to the final `return 1` branch, which I confirmed by stepping through the script.
violating_sentence: The red from the original assertion covers the rewritten one too, so the `-` expectation is known to catch an unlisted flag.
fixed_sentence: The rewritten assertion, run with the flag removed from the list, failed as well, so the `-` expectation is known to catch an unlisted flag.
why: The failure belonged to the original owner assertion but is credited to the rewritten `-` assertion. The fix reports a fresh red of the rewritten one.

paragraph: The guard treats the file as server-only, so every write arrives through the append call, and I confirmed that by watching a hand-edit get refused in the log. Nothing checks the field labels, though. My first test asserted that a body with no labels is rejected, and it failed because the call stored the body untouched. I narrowed the assertion to inspect only the heading line of the stored entry. Since the earlier assertion went red on the label-less body, the narrowed one on the heading line is also known to fail against the current guard.
violating_sentence: Since the earlier assertion went red on the label-less body, the narrowed one on the heading line is also known to fail against the current guard.
fixed_sentence: The narrowed assertion on the heading line, run against the current guard, also went red on the label-less body.
why: A failure of the broad assertion is used as evidence for the narrowed assertion, which was never run. The fix reports an observed red of the narrowed one.

paragraph: The scalar filter drops nested objects entirely: printing its output for a `find` payload showed no trace of the `hints` block, and the `_ => None` arm is the only path those objects take. For the regression test I first parsed the return value as JSON and checked a leaf. That assertion failed, because the function returns a plain string. I switched it to a substring check for `unindexed_files` in that string. The red from the JSON-parsing assertion stands as proof that the string assertion fails without the nested branch. Both callers then need a look, since each passes the string on unchanged.

fixed_sentence: Running the substring assertion before adding the nested branch also went red, so it fails without that branch.
why: The JSON-parsing assertion failed for a different reason (return type), yet it is cited for the edited substring assertion. The fix observes the edited one failing.

paragraph: The two filter engines disagree on `%`. The in-memory `eval` path does a case-insensitive substring test, and I confirmed that by feeding it a value with `%` in the middle and getting no match against text lacking a literal percent sign. My first test expected entry-grain filtering to act as a pattern, and it failed against that path. I rewrote it to expect literal matching and check the artifact-grain path against the same value. That red on the pattern assertion counts for the literal-text version as well, so the edited test is established as detecting the disagreement.
violating_sentence: That red on the pattern assertion counts for the literal-text version as well, so the edited test is established as detecting the disagreement.
fixed_sentence: The literal-text version, run against the artifact-grain path, failed on the same value, so the edited test detects the disagreement.
why: The failure of the pattern assertion is treated as evidence for the rewritten literal-text assertion. The fix cites a failure observed from the rewritten test.

paragraph: The served instructions file contains no retired tool name today, so this is a latent gap rather than a live defect. I checked by grepping the file for all eleven retired names and got zero hits. To close the gap I added a test asserting that none of them appear. When I planted `find_sym` in the file, the first draft of that test went red, as intended. I then rewrote the pattern to match on word boundaries, so that prose like "find symbols" would not trigger it. Since the first draft went red on the planted name, the word-boundary version is known to catch it too.

paragraph: The gate counted one conflicted file three times, because an unmerged path shows up as three index entries. A test that built a conflicted repo and asserted the file count equals the distinct path count went red, reporting 3 against 1. I then changed the assertion to compare against a set of paths and switched the collection to a `BTreeSet`. That red on the count comparison covers the set-based assertion as well. On the main checkout, the old and new collectors return identical output across 412 files, which I confirmed by diffing the two lists.
violating_sentence: That red on the count comparison covers the set-based assertion as well.
fixed_sentence: The set-based assertion also went red on the conflicted repo when run against the old collector.
why: The assertion was changed after its red, but the old red is treated as covering the new assertion; the fix observes the edited assertion failing.

paragraph: Two shell scripts still call a tool by its old parameter name, and no gate reads them: the test manifest lists no shell targets, so `cargo test` never touches them. I added a scan that greps the scripts for the parameter names in a hardcoded list. Run against a stale copy, it went red on `--path`. I then changed the scan to read parameter names from the schema JSON instead of the list. The schema-driven scan is proven to catch a stale parameter because the hardcoded one went red on one. Both scripts now sit under the scan.
violating_sentence: The schema-driven scan is proven to catch a stale parameter because the hardcoded one went red on one.
fixed_sentence: The schema-driven scan also went red on the stale `--path` copy when rerun against it.
why: The scan was rewritten after it failed, and the earlier red is cited for the new version; the fix reruns the edited scan and sees it fail.

paragraph: The doc comment holds for the mismatch direction: a sidecar stamped with sha A, read by a binary built at sha B, is rejected, and the test for that passes on every platform we run. The gap is the converse. I wrote a test asserting that equal shas mean the same build, and it went red when two builds, one from a dirty tree, shared a sha. I then reworded the assertion to require equal shas plus a clean-tree flag. The red from the equal-sha assertion carries over to the dirty-flag assertion, so the guard is known to reject dirty builds.
violating_sentence: The red from the equal-sha assertion carries over to the dirty-flag assertion, so the guard is known to reject dirty builds.
fixed_sentence: Rerunning the two builds with a shared sha turned the dirty-flag assertion red, so the guard rejects dirty builds.
why: The assertion was reworded after failing, and its earlier red is used for the new wording; the fix re-observes a red on the reworded assertion.

paragraph: The 101 from the earlier run shows the loosened assertion still rejects a bare `n=`. That run ended with `DEFAULT exit=101` in stdout, a real red from the test that forbids a bare `n=` in class field states, triggered by an uncommitted edit that bolded one. The author then loosened the test to accept the bolded form and handed the branch over. No `wip_authors` field came with the failure, so attribution was recovered by hand from the path in the failure text. The path led to the session that had made the edit.

fixed_sentence: A fresh run with a bare `n=` planted exited 101 under the loosened assertion, so it still rejects one.
why: The test was loosened after the red, yet the earlier exit 101 is cited for the loosened version; the fix plants a bare `n=` and observes a new red.

paragraph: The process-count check in the startup test expected 22 and reported 21 on Tuesday's run. The process table from that run is gone, so the cause stays open. I rewrote the assertion to expect 21 after the server/mux split, and the earlier red on the 22 version shows the new check would catch a mux that miscounts. Both pre-split logs list processes rather than threads, so the unit is settled even though the number is not. Re-derive the baseline from a fresh post-split run before trusting either figure.

paragraph: The mutation script seeds its worktree from HEAD plus the one file passed on the command line. Yesterday's test asserted that the NOTE lists every dirty file, and it failed on a two-file change because the NOTE named only one. I changed the assertion to compare against the files cargo actually needed, and yesterday's red already proves the new comparison detects the gap. The build log from that run shows the second file was required for the mutated module to compile, so the gap is real and the NOTE is blind to it.

paragraph: The slot-swap probe runs a one-shot claude call and then reads the slot file. The first version of the check compared the slot's session field against the id printed by the shell, and it failed because the slot held a different id. The json output shows the probe's id differs from the shell's, so that comparison could never pass. I switched the check to compare against the id inside out.json, and the red from the shell-id version counts as proof that this check fails when the slot is not swapped.
violating_sentence: I switched the check to compare against the id inside out.json, and the red from the shell-id version counts as proof that this check fails when the slot is not swapped.

paragraph: The ranking test failed on the May entry, so I rewrote it to sort by dependent count, and that earlier red already shows the rewrite catches a bad ordering. Each entry now carries a decay class and a pointer back to its proof. The doctor checks only read the tracker file; I confirmed this by running all four against a copy with write permission removed, and each completed. The stale list puts the August entry with forty dependents ahead of the one with three.
violating_sentence: The ranking test failed on the May entry, so I rewrote it to sort by dependent count, and that earlier red already shows the rewrite catches a bad ordering.
fixed_sentence: I rewrote the ranking test to sort by dependent count, then fed it a shuffled list and watched it fail on the May entry.

paragraph: The under-use test asserted that the agent never re-reads a file whose contents the tool result already contained. It went red on Claude in 9 of 12 trials. The tool result body was intact in every trial, so truncation is not the cause, and the transcripts show a fresh read within two turns each time. I then narrowed the assertion to count only reads of files under 200 lines, and the earlier 9-of-12 red backs up the narrowed version.
violating_sentence: I then narrowed the assertion to count only reads of files under 200 lines, and the earlier 9-of-12 red backs up the narrowed version.
fixed_sentence: I then narrowed the assertion to count only reads of files under 200 lines and reran all 12 trials, which went red in 7.

paragraph: The Windows shutdown test originally asserted that the child exits with code 0 within two seconds of the stop request. It failed on the CI runner, since taskkill gives the child no chance to return any exit code. I rewrote the assertion to check that no stale lock file remains in the workspace after shutdown. Tuesday's failure therefore shows the lock-file check catches the forced-kill path. The Linux run of the same test passes, and its log shows the lock file removed by the server's own SIGTERM handler before exit. The Windows job still needs a graceful path before that check can go green.
violating_sentence: Tuesday's failure therefore shows the lock-file check catches the forced-kill path.
fixed_sentence: Rerunning the lock-file check on the runner failed with a stale lock left after the forced kill.
why: The earlier red belonged to the exit-code assertion, which was then rewritten; the sentence treats it as evidence for the lock-file check. The fix reports a re-observed failure.

paragraph: The integration test for library-scoped reference search first expected hits from a sibling checkout that is not a declared dependency. It failed with zero results, and the server log shows no index entries for the sibling path, so the server evidently indexes only the workspace and its resolved dependencies. I then narrowed the assertion to expect only hits inside resolved dependency jars. The tool description now tells agents not to expect cross-project discovery. The zero-result failure from the sibling query means the narrowed assertion is already known to fail when the server returns nothing.
violating_sentence: The zero-result failure from the sibling query means the narrowed assertion is already known to fail when the server returns nothing.
fixed_sentence: Pointing the narrowed assertion at a server stub that returns nothing made it fail, as intended.
why: The zero-result red came from the earlier sibling-checkout assertion, not the narrowed one; the fix re-observes a failure of the edited assertion.

paragraph: The question-count check now allows two questions, and the failure logged last week counts as proof that it rejects a third. That failure came from the original limit of one question, when the transcript showed two multiple-choice prompts before the brief. The rest of the transcript is fine: the skill announced itself, inferred a Rust async project, and showed the brief. After confirmation, the call to the research tool carried summary mode, three queries and five sources, matching the argument list in the expected flow.
violating_sentence: The question-count check now allows two questions, and the failure logged last week counts as proof that it rejects a third.
fixed_sentence: The question-count check now allows two questions, and a replayed transcript with three prompts fails it.

paragraph: The credential guard in the pilot script is worth copying as it stands. Both eval profiles share one symlinked credential, and an OAuth refresh swaps the symlink for a regular file, which is what broke three profiles in August. My first test asserted the link survives a refresh, and it failed, as expected. I then edited it to accept a regular file with matching contents. The failure from the symlink assertion covers the new regular-file check as well. Before the pilot starts, back up the output directory, because its logs are the only record of each ruling.
violating_sentence: The failure from the symlink assertion covers the new regular-file check as well.
fixed_sentence: After the edit, I forced a refresh with a stale token and the regular-file check failed as expected.
why: The red belonged to the symlink assertion, which was then edited; the sentence extends it to the new check. The fix re-observes a red on the edited assertion.

paragraph: The diagnostic log now gets a file layer at INFO level, with a random four-character instance ID in its name, so parallel servers never share a file. The heartbeat test asserts that a heartbeat line appears in that file. With a ten-second window it failed, since the heartbeat interval is thirty seconds and the log held no lines yet. I widened the window to thirty-five seconds. The ten-second failure shows the widened check would fail if the heartbeat were disabled.

paragraph: The stale-context bug showed up when two projects were activated in one session and the second one kept answering from the first one's paths. I wrote a test that activates project A, then project B, and asserts that derive_ctx returns B's root. It failed on the first run, returning A's root, which confirmed the cache was serving stale entries. After that I rewrote the assertion to compare the full context object, including git_root, instead of only the root path. Since the earlier run already failed, the rewritten assertion is confirmed to catch the stale cache. Removing the cache entirely made the original root-path check pass, and per-call cost stayed in the hundreds of microseconds, so the cache is not worth keeping.

fixed_sentence: Since the earlier failure came from the old root-path assertion, the rewritten full-context assertion still needs its own failing run against the cache.

paragraph: The friction probe needs three derived columns, and each has a different source. friction_target is read from the row's input directly, because the full input_json is debug-gated and the test record_content_no_input_in_normal_mode shows it is None in normal mode. err_family is a pure function of error_msg, so storing it as a column lets the probe be a plain GROUP BY. For overflow_tokens, the envelope must carry the size. My test for it originally asserted the field equals the buffered length, and it failed with a missing-key error. I then changed the assertion to compare against the JSON length of the payload, and that failure shows the envelope lacks the size field. Once the one-field addition lands, the recorder can read it.

fixed_sentence: I then changed the assertion to compare against the JSON length of the payload, and its own run failed with the same missing-key error.

paragraph: The blind second read was Claude reading Claude, with the same model family and the same stylistic attractors, so the 86% agreement partly measures shared bias. Classification, promotion, and verdicts all run through one operator and one model lineage. To test whether redaction removed the giveaways, I wrote a check that a reader could name the author from redacted text, and it passed on the first draft, meaning authorship was guessable. I then tightened the check to require a match on three stylistic markers rather than one. The tightened check has already shown that redaction leaks authorship, since the first draft failed to hold. Every agreement figure should be bounded accordingly.
