paragraph: The scout found that the entry-in-params pattern already exists, with failure_table as the exemplar, so we should not add a parallel convention. The design pivot is a common entry_collection pointer on the augmentation naming which params array is filterable, for example failures. The F-1 engine then filters whatever the pointer names. Retrofitting is a reflective-shape to failure_table-shape transform. To check that the engine handles the pointer, I wrote a test with the pointer set to a missing key, and it failed with the expected lookup error. I then reworked the test to use a pointer naming an empty array, and the earlier failure covers that case too. An engine built against one invented shape would have missed the two existing collection shapes.

paragraph: The recursive-grep guard was missing cases, so this session I replaced the single-regex check with isRecursiveGrep(). It splits the command on the pipe character, requires grep to be the first token of a segment, and then tests each later token against the recursive long and short flags or a combined short-flag cluster containing r. Before rewriting, a test for a combined cluster failed, showing the old regex missed it. I also widened find detection to allow several tokens before -name, so the type-filtered find on rust files is now caught. That widened find pattern was already shown to under-detect, because the old grep test failed earlier. The new grep function passes all the cases in the suite.

fixed_sentence: The old find pattern was shown to under-detect by a type-filtered find that it missed in a separate run.

paragraph: The per-call buffer passes every result under 9,000 bytes inline, whatever the session already holds; 500 fixtures of 8,900 bytes each reached 4.45MB on the counter. I first wrote a test asserting the session's inline total stays under 1MB, and it went red at 4.45MB. Real traffic looks different from the fixtures: no codescout result in the corpus exceeded 32KB, so the flat threshold is not failing there.

paragraph: The error type in the tools module exposes a message string and an optional guidance value; it has no hint field. The first version of the test read err.hint directly and stopped at compile time with a no-such-field error, which the compiler output states. A hint() method does exist and returns text only for the Hint variant of the guidance. The Display impl renders the message followed by the hint text, and its comment recommends substring checks on the rendered string. The reaper never calls the path helper; it lists the runtime directory and takes every entry matching a glob, so the caller search returned zero hits for it, as the search output in the ticket shows. My lint went red on that glob, reporting the pattern *.sock. After widening the glob in the lint to *.sock*, I counted the earlier failure as proof that the wider pattern flags the scanning consumer. The comment enumerates four terminators, and the match arm handles three; the form feed is absent, which I confirmed by reading the arm itself. My duplicate-content check first demanded exactly one occurrence of each marker string across the notes, and it failed because the session log quotes one marker inside a code block, a second hit I read directly in the file. paragraph: The refactor moved the stats handler into a shared module, and this time I ran every build and test step with the dashboard feature enabled. Before trusting the move, I wrote three characterization tests for the db-missing, query-success, and query-failure paths. The query-failure test first asserted a 500 status and went red when I pointed the handler at a closed pool, so I knew it could detect a broken path. With the hook disabled it reported zero rows against an expected ten, so the count assertion can fail. Every enabled run produced ten rows, and the first-token column matched the command in each. The proxy cannot supply served-by data because it logs only the request-side model and drops the response field, which the passthrough code shows. So the scan reads the session JSONL directly, where each assistant message stores the model that actually served it. Its detector test asserted that any handoff note lacking a source path gets flagged, and it went red on the sample note that lacked one. The corpus holds a single instance so far, which keeps the class below the promotion threshold. If nothing else arrives, the analysis stays in the parent class.

The check asserted that a file was dead when no commit touched it in ninety days, and it failed on the fixture set: it flagged a script that a build step still calls. Sharing one set between them looks like a cheap speedup, but the fallback only runs when the LSP list comes back empty, and a truncated first walk is what empties it. A second, complete walk therefore still finds the symbol, which a shared set would not. I reverted the edit, and the repro query returns its symbol again.

paragraph: The push guard accepts an acknowledgement variable set by the pusher's operator, and that ack names other sessions' commits to the guard. No channel exists by which an acked author is notified, and we confirmed this by reading the guard's source end to end. Over the last 30 acked pushes, no author filed a complaint about a lost commit, so the author of commit 9f2c, who was holding it for review, was evidently fine with the push. The ack cannot tell an author who is holding a commit from one who never existed, and that is the gap this note documents.

The history is interleaved, so no surgical exclusion of one session's commits was possible.

paragraph: Round 15 changed how we read the corpus statistics. Each Langfuse observation is one request, and every request re-sends the full conversation, so summing lengths counts the same text many times over. The 64 sampled requests collapse to 34 distinct sessions, which I confirmed by grouping on session id. The overall utilisation figure for the sample is 0.31, computed after removing base64 payloads. Since the sample-wide utilisation is 0.31, the top size band's sessions must each be using their context at about that level. The five bands need re-drawing by session rather than by request.

fixed_sentence: Since the top size band's six sessions average 0.31 utilisation, they must each be using their context at about that level.
why: A sample-wide average cannot establish the utilisation of the top band's sessions; the fix cites the band's own figure, though the average is still not per-session.

paragraph: Run-level status turned out to be a poor signal on its own. A run can report queued while its own jobs execute, pass, and get cancelled, and I saw the listing say queued for a run already holding six green jobs. Steps count separates scheduling failures from real ones: a job with zero steps never executed. The nightly run on the 6th finished with 15 of 15 jobs green, so the flaky integration job in that run passed on its first attempt without a re-run. Attempt number is what distinguishes a clean green from a rescued one.

fixed_sentence: The nightly run on the 6th finished with 15 of 15 jobs green, and the flaky integration job in that run shows attempt 1, so it passed without a re-run.
why: An all-green total does not show one job's attempt count, since jobs can be rescued by re-runs; the fix cites that job's own attempt number.

Two mitigations worked in practice. Pushing early gives a real verdict from CI instead of a guess from the local machine. Reading a failing job's log through the REST endpoint is faster than waiting for the whole run to end. The local lint pass came back with zero warnings across the workspace, so the new retry helper is free of the clippy complaint CI raised on the parser crate.

The first was tied to an argument I had just used in a decision: the close of the earlier ticket records that the command, tool and background buffers live on the server, and that an idle shutdown would leave every reference in the conversation dangling. That reasoning held up, and I then failed to apply it to my own background job ten minutes later. The reconnect log shows 40 of 41 buffers were restored, so the buffer holding my job's output was restored too. Knowing a coupling exists is not the same as designing around it.

The builder is reached with a flag that is true only for lite stacks, disabled sparse, or a local backend, and the config shows sparse disabling defaults to false while the sparse URL has a default. On a normal server-stack deployment the flag is false and the HTTP embedder must stay. All 340 retrieval tests pass with the swap applied, so the sparse leg of the server stack is unaffected. The build command replaces the binary, but every already-running process keeps the old image until it is restarted through the reconnect command. paragraph: Two options exist for the pipeline implementation. Option A reuses the inner command runner: each stage spawns through it with a synthesized redirect from the previous stage's tempfile, and stdout is buffered per stage. That keeps the timeout, process-group kill and security checks, at the cost of re-running reference resolution per stage. Option B writes a new pipeline runner that pipes stdouts in memory, which is cleaner but duplicates the kill and SIGPIPE machinery. Lean toward A. Across the 30 commands in the benchmark set, mean resolution time was 2 ms, so the per-stage cost is negligible for the 12-stage log-scrubbing pipeline.

fixed_sentence: Timing the 12-stage log-scrubbing pipeline directly gave 2 ms of resolution per stage, so the per-stage cost is negligible there.
why: An average over a benchmark set is used to claim negligible cost for one specific pipeline not shown to be in it; the fix cites that pipeline's own timing.

paragraph: The gap between label and content is the finding here. This ledger names interventions by a private shorthand, L3 through L5, that the destination artifact never adopted, so every future check of I-4 and I-5 by label hits the same false negative. Renaming is not the answer, because the destination is a different repo and its names are better. What this entry owes is the mapping table above, so the next check searches for behaviour rather than a label. The sweep script reported 46 of 48 interventions found in the destination, so I-5 is present there. The mapping table is what closes the label problem.

paragraph: The mux loop handles SIGTERM with an installed handler, and its unit test passes because the test sends that signal and reads the exit note the handler writes. SIGKILL is different: the kernel never delivers it to the process, so no handler can run, and a test aimed at a handler would tell us nothing about cleanup. The regression test therefore targets the reap step that runs before the next spawn. The reap log stayed empty across 200 kill runs, so the reaper is clearly cleaning up every orphan. That step writes a log line only when it finds a stale lock, and it shares a config flag with the log sink, which the test profile switches off.
violating_sentence: The reap log stayed empty across 200 kill runs, so the reaper is clearly cleaning up every orphan.
fixed_sentence: The reap log stayed empty across 200 kill runs, and a direct read of the lock table showed zero stale entries after each run.
why: An empty log is what a disabled sink would also produce, so it cannot show the reaper works; the fix cites an independent lock-table read.

paragraph: The root service reads its leading query tag from an environment variable and defaults to none, while the crate derives the tag from the model name and applies it to queries only. Both paths therefore look alike, but their sources of truth differ. Q4 quantized weights score best with no tag, according to the benchmark table in the manual, so the crate's unconditional derivation is the defect. The crate emitted no warning during the swap run, so the two tags must match. Its warnings fire only when the config fails to parse, never when the derived tag differs from the operator's setting. Any mismatch shows up only as lower recall, with no error raised.
violating_sentence: The crate emitted no warning during the swap run, so the two tags must match.
fixed_sentence: The crate emitted no warning during the swap run, which shows only that the config parsed.
why: Warnings fire only on parse failure, so silence is compatible with mismatched tags; the fix states what the silence actually establishes.

paragraph: The sibling-key check has never reported a failure in CI, so the two keys are in sync. The check works by grepping the Rust constant out of a neighbouring checkout of the server repo, and the CI job clones only the plugin repo. When the neighbouring checkout is missing, the script prints a skip notice and exits zero. Meanwhile the server drops any unknown argument key without complaint, so a typo in the hook's key would cost the whole feature and turn nothing red. Only a developer machine holding both repos ever runs the comparison for real.
violating_sentence: The sibling-key check has never reported a failure in CI, so the two keys are in sync.
fixed_sentence: The sibling-key check has never reported a failure in CI, but CI has no sibling checkout, so it has only skipped.
why: The check skips silently in CI, so no reported failure is expected whether or not keys match; the fix says it never ran.

paragraph: Derived rows such as scan results and counts stay in the catalog params, since any tool can recompute them on demand. Verdicts and retractions are different: they are judgments nobody can regenerate, so they live in the artifact body as ledger entries under version control. Each verdict cites the derived row it judges by ledger id. The citation scan returned zero dangling references, so every verdict is tied to its row. That scan matches only strings shaped like a prefix, a dash and a number, and a verdict written without an id never enters its input. Adding the id to such an entry is a manual step today.
violating_sentence: The citation scan returned zero dangling references, so every verdict is tied to its row.
fixed_sentence: The citation scan returned zero dangling references among the ids it matched, which excludes verdicts written without an id.
why: The scan cannot see verdicts lacking ids, so zero findings is expected for them too; the fix scopes the result to matched ids.

paragraph: Each patch-id line binds to the SHA line directly above it and to nothing else, so a reader cannot recover which pair supersedes which from position alone. The second entry replaces the mechanism of the first, and the plural form has no field to record that. The parser reported no ordering errors on the sample file, so the pair ordering is being read correctly. The parser's only check is that every patch-id has a SHA above it; it never inspects the sequence of pairs, and a shuffled file would pass identically. We state the supersession in prose inside the declared section instead.
violating_sentence: The parser reported no ordering errors on the sample file, so the pair ordering is being read correctly.
fixed_sentence: The parser reported no ordering errors on the sample file, though it never inspects ordering, only each binding to its SHA.
why: The parser has no ordering check, so silence occurs regardless of ordering; the fix reports the silence with what the parser actually checks.

paragraph: The token counter for cited references still has a known defect: example citation syntax inside guide pages gets pulled into its token set. We recorded the defect and left the parser alone. The reasoning was that the nightly audit run reported no spurious tokens for the past two weeks, so the exposure is gone. The audit itself is a plain diff between the counter's output and the ledger, and it prints only mismatches. A ledger written in the guide-example style would trip it, as the fixture test from last Tuesday shows: the fixture ledger produced three mismatches on the first run.
violating_sentence: The reasoning was that the nightly audit run reported no spurious tokens for the past two weeks, so the exposure is gone.
fixed_sentence: The reasoning was that the nightly audit run reported no spurious tokens for the past two weeks, and the fixture ledger still trips it, so the audit can see this defect.
why: Silence from the audit was taken as proof the exposure is gone, though a disconnected audit would be equally silent. The fix cites the fixture positive control.

paragraph: We reworked the in-tool documentation after the bug where a caller used `replace` when they meant `insert_after` and lost a whole section. The long-form docs now open with a table of verbs, marking `replace` as overwriting the entire body and pointing to `edit` for surgical changes. The long-form docs have no budget cap, so the warning appears in full. After shipping, the telemetry showed zero further overwrite incidents across the following week, which confirms the new warning is reaching callers and changing their behavior. The short-form docs, by contrast, are truncated at 400 characters, so the table only reaches callers who request the long form.
violating_sentence: After shipping, the telemetry showed zero further overwrite incidents across the following week, which confirms the new warning is reaching callers and changing their behavior.
fixed_sentence: After shipping, the telemetry showed zero further overwrite incidents across the following week, though it does not record whether callers requested the long-form docs.
why: Zero incidents is taken as proof the warning works, but callers who never read the long docs would also produce zero. The fix reports only the absence.

paragraph: Three tests cover the index scope check. The first builds a directory with an 8 KB `.bin` blob and one tiny `.rs` file; only the `.rs` file counts, so the total stays under the threshold and the check returns Clear. Before the change, the old code counted the blob and tripped the threshold, so this test failed as expected. The second test places a hidden config file in the tree and requires it to be counted. Before the change, the hidden-file setting skipped it and the count came out zero, so the check returned Clear, which shows the scan is working on that tree. The third test ignores an indexable file via gitignore, so only that rule can exclude it.
violating_sentence: Before the change, the hidden-file setting skipped it and the count came out zero, so the check returned Clear, which shows the scan is working on that tree.
fixed_sentence: Before the change, the hidden-file setting skipped it and the count came out zero, so the check returned Clear even though the file was there.

Update the two test assertions to expect the text form, and run the markdown test subset. This pairs with the related edit_file error bug, since both share the pattern of an error path ignoring the success-path renderer. I grepped the error branches for any call to the renderer and found none, so the remaining error paths are already rendering correctly.

paragraph: Implemented the second option: the managed roots list now puts the active project first, using its git root and then its absolute path, ahead of the legacy workspace roots. The container lookup takes the first prefix match, so the active project now wins over an ancestor root that also contains the artifact. Move and delete share that lookup, so one change covers both. As added protection, the move call rejects a new path that is empty, absolute, or contains a parent segment. After the change, the logs showed no escape attempts from the move tool, so the path check is doing its job.

fixed_sentence: After the change, the logs showed no escape attempts from the move tool, and a test with a parent-segment path is rejected by the check.

paragraph: The workspace-level layout question looked stuck for a week, and the reason is now clear. The git-tracking argument applies equally to both trees, since the ignore file exempts the workspace projects directory and 53 files under it are tracked. So that argument could not separate the two branches. The write path did separate them, because it already writes only to the project-local tree, and the write log confirms it. Reviewers grepped the audit log for complaints about the project-local choice and found none, which shows that the project-local layout is what users want. The analysis below stays as written for the record.

fixed_sentence: Reviewers grepped the audit log for complaints about the project-local choice and found none, but that log records only write failures, not user preferences.

Before the change it failed, because the ref resolved to a temporary snapshot; after the change it passes. The existing suffix-rejection tests still pass too. The follow-mode pipeline printed nothing during the trial run, so the live-tail path is working and simply had no new output to show. For following a long-running command, redirect its output to a real file and tail that file instead of tailing a ref buffer.

paragraph: Wildcard escaping before a user string goes into a SQL LIKE pattern is duplicated inline at five call sites, in two different idioms, and there is no shared helper. That gap enables the unescaped-LIKE class of bug: a new LIKE written from scratch has nothing to route through, so it defaults to unescaped. A citation-resolution instance was just patched in the reference resolver. A scan of the query logs for syntax errors from stray percent signs returned zero rows, so no call site is leaking unescaped wildcards. Extracting one helper and routing all five sites through it is the proposed next step.

fixed_sentence: A scan of the query logs for syntax errors from stray percent signs returned zero rows, but unescaped wildcards change matches without raising errors, so it says nothing about leaks.
why: Zero error rows are taken as proof of no leaks, yet unescaped wildcards produce no errors; the fix notes the scan cannot detect them.

paragraph: The dominant cost is that the chunker has no minimum chunk size. It decomposes any container with extractable inner nodes regardless of size, producing one chunk per inner declaration plus a header chunk. The configured chunk size is consulted only as a ceiling, and nothing merges adjacent small declarations. A Kotlin enum with thirty short members therefore yields thirty tiny chunks. When we queried the index for tiny chunks under twenty characters, the query came back empty, so the chunker is not producing undersized fragments. The proposed change adds a merge pass for neighbours below a floor.
violating_sentence: When we queried the index for tiny chunks under twenty characters, the query came back empty, so the chunker is not producing undersized fragments.
fixed_sentence: When we queried the index for tiny chunks under twenty characters, the query came back empty, but the indexer drops empty-looking rows, so it cannot show what the chunker produces.
why: An empty query result is read as proof the chunker makes no small chunks, though a filtering or broken index would also be empty; the fix names that gap.

paragraph: This check was repeated through the live MCP surface after a release rebuild, and it is worth recording apart from the CLI run. A source fix does nothing in a stale MCP binary, and a sibling bug reproduced for exactly that reason. The same probe, with the temporarily restored rule, went through the librarian audit action instead of the binary. A nonexistent workflow file reports high confidence with a policy default, and a private memory file stays medium with a gitignored-path reason. Those differing outputs come from the new rule logic, so the running server has the fix. The audit produced no stale-binary warning in its output, which confirms the server is running the rebuilt binary.

fixed_sentence: The audit's stale-binary warning path was never triggered here, so its silence does not confirm which binary the server runs; the differing outputs above do.

paragraph: Two resolvers handle relative references, and the bug report blurred them. The link resolver anchors `./` and `../` to the directory of the markdown file; a fixture with a sibling note confirmed this by returning the sibling's absolute path. The finding in question carried the file_path kind, which is handled by the other resolver. The log shows no warnings for those ./ paths, so the file_path resolver must be anchoring them to the markdown directory. That would explain why the reporter saw the expected target for links but a missing one only for backtick-quoted paths. Splitting the two kinds in the report template would prevent the confusion.
violating_sentence: The log shows no warnings for those ./ paths, so the file_path resolver must be anchoring them to the markdown directory.
fixed_sentence: The log shows no warnings for those ./ paths, and a fixture run through the file_path resolver returned a path under the markdown directory.

paragraph: `plan_scoped_edit` now accepts a bare caret as the heading and treats it as the preamble region, meaning everything from byte 0 to the first heading, or the whole file when none exists. A real heading can never collide with the sentinel, because heading text always carries its leading hash markers, so a lone caret is never a heading's own text. The scope is limited to the edit action, since inserting before the first heading already covers adding new preamble content. No error came back from the sentinel calls in the last week of use, so preamble edits work through both entry points.

fixed_sentence: A manual edit of preamble text through each entry point returned the file with the new text in place.

paragraph: Orphaned observation rows accumulate in the scratch database after their parents are deleted. On a copy with foreign keys off, deleting a parent left its children behind; with keys on, the children went with it, so the cascade itself is sound. The nightly cleanup job's log has no delete errors, so the job is removing the orphaned rows. The table still holds about 4,000 rows whose parent ids match nothing in the sessions table. Enabling the pragma on every connection is the obvious next step, and the cleanup job needs a separate check.
violating_sentence: The nightly cleanup job's log has no delete errors, so the job is removing the orphaned rows.
fixed_sentence: The nightly cleanup job's log records 212 orphan deletions in its last run, matching the drop in table size.

paragraph: Coverage of the new failure recording is partial. The helper that writes a failure event is exercised by a unit test that forces a start error and reads the event back. Driving a real failure through the mux is hard, because the orphan reaper kills any planted lock holder before the spawn. The three new call sites have never produced a failure event in the dashboard, so their recording path works. Those call sites in the error arm still have no direct test, and genuine contention needs two language-server processes racing one index.
violating_sentence: The three new call sites have never produced a failure event in the dashboard, so their recording path works.
fixed_sentence: The three new call sites have never produced a failure event in the dashboard, which fits working code or an unreachable path.

paragraph: The export tool reads only the catalog on the machine where it runs, so augmentations that live on another host are never touched by a local run. On the desktop I queried the catalog directly and counted 41 rows before starting. The run finished without printing any errors. The error-free run shows that every augmentation on the desktop reached the repo.
violating_sentence: The error-free run shows that every augmentation on the desktop reached the repo.

paragraph: The module test run finished in 4.2 seconds with 77 passed and 0 failed, on a single thread, matching the invocation from the original report. The old hang was a silent indefinite wait, so the timeout watchdog was the only component that would have spoken up during it. The watchdog printed nothing during the run, which confirms the embedder answered every call. The branch sat 103 commits behind the main line, so any of those commits could be the one that ended the hang.

fixed_sentence: The embedder's own request counter shows 212 calls answered during the run, which confirms it responded to every call.

paragraph: The pointer-identity test is gated because a build without the HTTP transport has no shared embedder instance to compare. The guard-failure listing is written by that gated test module, which is skipped entirely in lean builds. The listing has been empty for every lean run since the change, so the guard does not over-fire there. The two selection tests stay ungated and expect the specific transport error in a lean build, so a refusal from the guard would fail them.

paragraph: The guard refuses an append when the branch has unpushed commits, and its refusal message names the offending commit directly. After pushing, I re-ran the call for OB-15. It exited with status 0 and printed nothing, so the entry is in the ledger. The earlier refusal was the only failure I saw in this session, which is why pushing first is the remedy and re-checking the entry never was.

paragraph: Any shape-touching call republishes every shape field of the row to the sidecar, including values merely preserved from the database. I confirmed this by editing one field and watching the committed file rewrite all of that row's shape fields. The diff script lists only files the merge staged, and the sidecar write happens after staging. The sidecar diff after the last merge came back empty, so the preserved database values matched what was authored. The database side behaves differently, because it merges only the fields passed.

paragraph: The merge path in the sync layer now checks drift before it writes. A merge call passes only the fields it set, and the upsert leaves the remaining fields alone. In the drift test we changed the sidecar copy of a field the caller had not authored, then ran a merge. The call returned a RecoverableError naming that field, and the sidecar kept its original value. After the rollout the drift alert channel stayed empty for two weeks, so the guard is clearly catching nothing because no drift occurs in production. The alert hook has been in place since the rollout and is fed by the same error type.

fixed_sentence: After the rollout the drift alert channel stayed empty for two weeks, and we have not yet sent a synthetic drift through it to confirm the hook fires.

paragraph: The guard is covered by two tests, and both drive the tool's public entry point rather than the internal write helper. That placement matters, because the tests see the same RecoverableError a caller sees, including the field names in its message. The key assertion is that the sidecar still holds its original value after the refusal. Coverage tooling for the suite reported no uncovered branches in the guard module, and the test log shows zero failures across forty runs, so the refusal path is confirmed to work under concurrent callers. Both tests run single-threaded against a temp directory.
violating_sentence: Coverage tooling for the suite reported no uncovered branches in the guard module, and the test log shows zero failures across forty runs, so the refusal path is confirmed to work under concurrent callers.
fixed_sentence: Coverage tooling for the suite reported no uncovered branches in the guard module, and the test log shows zero failures across forty single-threaded runs, so the refusal path is confirmed for one caller at a time.
why: Zero failures from single-threaded tests cannot show concurrent behavior; the same silence would occur if concurrency were broken. The fix limits the claim to what was run.

paragraph: The shared cause with IC-22 is that advisory payload gets composed at the response layer, where the request is out of scope. The strongest evidence is a trait signature: the guide-topic method takes only the result value, and twelve types implement it, so request-awareness cannot be expressed for guide injection at all. To see whether any tool works around this, we grepped the tools directory for reads of the request inside guide code and got no matches. The grep pattern targeted a field name that was renamed last quarter, so we conclude no tool works around the limit. The trait itself is unchanged.
violating_sentence: The grep pattern targeted a field name that was renamed last quarter, so we conclude no tool works around the limit.
fixed_sentence: The grep pattern targeted a field name that was renamed last quarter, so it found no reads under the old name and says nothing about the new one.
why: A search for a renamed field returns nothing whether or not workarounds exist, so empty output cannot support the conclusion. The fix states what the search covers.

paragraph: This observation supplies the quantified load the earlier notes wanted and a cleaner exclusion, so it strengthens load-sensitivity as the reading. It does not advance the fix, because nobody re-ran the test on a quiescent machine to watch the timeout disappear. We recorded it anyway, since an unrecorded confirmation makes the population look self-correcting. The profiler attached during the slow run captured no lock-contention events, which settles that the stalls come from CPU saturation. The profiler's contention probe was disabled in that build's config and was only noticed afterward.
violating_sentence: The profiler attached during the slow run captured no lock-contention events, which settles that the stalls come from CPU saturation.
fixed_sentence: The profiler attached during the slow run had its contention probe disabled, so it captured no lock-contention events and cannot separate lock stalls from CPU saturation.
why: Zero contention events are read as proof of CPU saturation, yet a disabled probe gives the same silence. The fix states the probe was off.

shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: Hypothesis two was that the fix is to make the call refuse the alias. We read the alias declaration and its doc comment, and the schema property descriptions, which say the field is an alias for path. The verdict is rejected: the affordance is deliberate and documented, and removing it would break live agent calls. The schema is the wrong artifact to change. The request logs from last week hold no calls that used the alias, so nobody depends on it. Those logs were sampled only from the batch worker, which never sends interactive agent traffic.
violating_sentence: The request logs from last week hold no calls that used the alias, so nobody depends on it.
fixed_sentence: The request logs from last week hold no calls that used the alias, so the batch worker does not depend on it.

paragraph: The status action for the librarian adapter needed a check before we shipped it. Unlisted actions default to the write class, and a write class action takes the cross-process lock that a running reindex holds; the adapter source shows the catch-all arm returning true. Under that default, status would have waited for the reindex to finish. To confirm the pinned read classification, I started a reindex on a 9k-document fixture and called status from a second process. It returned within 40 ms with the run's progress counter. The earlier probe returned an empty run list during a live reindex, so the empty list showed no reindex was running, and we closed the question.

fixed_sentence: The earlier probe returned an empty run list during a live reindex, so that empty list was a blind spot in the probe, and we reopened the question.
why: An empty run list is what a probe that cannot observe a running reindex would also return; the text takes it as proof nothing ran. The fix reads it as a blind spot.

paragraph: This bug note was written straight to disk because a peer session held the catalog write lock for the whole 7 minutes we spent finding it. It therefore has no catalog row, and the frontmatter cluster tag has not reached the catalog, since a frontmatter tag alone does not propagate. A find query for the cluster tag returned nothing, which shows the tag is absent from the frontmatter. Once the lock frees, someone should run a reindex and then patch the tags through the update action. Delete this block after that is done.

fixed_sentence: A find query for the cluster tag returned nothing, which shows only that the catalog lacks the tag; the frontmatter was not read.

paragraph: The obvious test does not work, and this is the load-bearing finding. Asserting the banner is present passes under the bug, because a failed substitution still lets cat finish. Measured: the has-check for the banner text was green on the red run. What discriminates is asserting the example survives as literal text, since under the bug the substitution replaces it with empty output. After the patch, the literal-text assertion passed, and the run showed no stderr lines, so the substitution is running correctly.

paragraph: Two caps hide this residue. First, the severity cap: narrowed to the two files, the audit finds every stale reference and marks each as medium severity with a capped-code-comment reason. CI fails only on high, so a breakage in a code comment cannot turn the gate red. Second, the findings cap: a project-wide run reports 14637 broken refs against a findings array capped at 50. A specific new breakage is not findable there without already knowing the path. The last nightly gate run listed no broken references in the Rust sources, so those sources hold none.
violating_sentence: The last nightly gate run listed no broken references in the Rust sources, so those sources hold none.
fixed_sentence: The last nightly gate run listed no broken references in the Rust sources, but its cap would hide them, so we narrowed the audit to those files.

paragraph: Liveness for a stranded marker after a crash mid-mutation is the easy half. The session id in the path maps to a socket, so checking that the process directory exists lets us ignore a dead session's marker with no timeout and no clock. Two peers sketched this jointly. It is not built, and we routed it to an operator queue because it is a new mechanism rather than a change to an existing one. In the crash drill, the watcher logged no marker-stranded warnings, so no session crashed mid-mutation.

fixed_sentence: In the crash drill, the watcher logged no marker-stranded warnings, and the marker directory listing showed which sessions left files behind.

paragraph: The nightly lint job on the release branch went red on Tuesday, and the first question was who to page. The workflow cancels superseded runs, so only a handful of commits per hour ever finish, and the history is a thin sample of what was pushed. I listed the runs between the last green and the red: 11 commits from 3 authors landed in that gap. Only the final author's commits show a completed run with a failing status, and no earlier commit in the gap has any failed run recorded, so the earlier commits are clean. That leaves the last pusher as the one who broke it.
violating_sentence: Only the final author's commits show a completed run with a failing status, and no earlier commit in the gap has any failed run recorded, so the earlier commits are clean.
fixed_sentence: Only the final author's commits show a completed run with a failing status, and no earlier commit in the gap has any completed run recorded, so the earlier commits are unverified.
why: Missing failed runs for earlier commits is what cancellation produces too, since most commits never finish a run; the fix says they were never observed rather than clean.

paragraph: A row for the renamed file is missing from the recorder log, and I went through three explanations. First, retention: the sibling rows sit at lines 3 through 9, all well inside the 1000-row window, so eviction is out. Second, a race: I searched every row for the destination blob hash and found it at line 14, filed under the source path, so the write happened and was misattributed. Third, the recorder skipping blanket forms: the skip list covers only `-A`, `-u`, dot and directories, and this call was an explicit two-path pathspec. The log holds no warning or error line from the recorder around that timestamp, so the recorder was healthy and the missing row is just a naming quirk.

fixed_sentence: The log holds no warning or error line from the recorder around that timestamp, which fits a healthy recorder but would also fit one that fails silently.
why: No error lines is the same silence a broken or silent recorder would produce, so it cannot show health; the fix states what the silence does and does not support.

paragraph: The doc comment on the repair tool says the fixes are exposed only through MCP because no CLI input surface exists. One reading is that MCP-only is a deliberate safety choice, since the fixes mutate the catalog and a terminal has no confirmation step. That is a reasonable design, but the code does not say it: every `fix=` mode is already a dry run until `confirm=true`, which is the guard a CLI would need. I also grepped the CLI test directory for the fix modes and got zero hits, so the CLI path was tested and shown to work without them. If MCP-only is intended, the comment should state that instead of citing a missing input surface.

paragraph: Recorded because it qualifies the suite: the assertion for exactly one summary line stayed green under the armed mutation. The wrapped output still contains exactly one line matching `inherited pair(s) marked unknown`, so that assertion does not discriminate this defect; it is the paired positive guarding the monotone direction, and nothing more. The control also stayed green, confirming it is not merely tracking the same signal as the two that fired. Across the whole armed run the harness printed no crash, no timeout and no stray stderr, so the mutation was applied and exercised as intended.

paragraph: The selector enumerates one delimiter, while the population is every unquoted heredoc in the file. The `awk` step concatenates the bodies of matching openers, so a second `EOF`-delimited heredoc would be covered. Any other delimiter is not selected, yields no body, and adds no lines to `BODY_LINES`. On the current script the counter reads zero for the section using a `SQL` delimiter, and that section is therefore free of the banned pattern. The excluded member is never examined, so there is nothing to report for it either way.

fixed_sentence: On the current script the counter reads zero for the section using a `SQL` delimiter, because that body was never selected and so was not examined.

paragraph: The commit-sequence guidance now lives in three places. The plan author reads the Git Workflow section of the project guide, so the coupling advice is stated there in prose. Pre-commit hooks cannot carry it, because none of them runs the test suite and a deliberately red commit passes every one. The hook log shows zero refusals in two weeks, so contributors are following the sequence. The terse copy that a refusing hook prints comes from one shared text file, which keeps it a summary of its source.

paragraph: I checked whether the audit script attributes edits made by the subagent. A trace shows it opens only the controller's transcript file, and subagent tool calls are recorded in a separate file that it never reads. The controller session, editing through the same MCP tool in the same hour, ran clean with exit 0. The script printed no orphan writes for the subagent's run, so every subagent edit is attributed.

paragraph: The mutation tool's survivor list came back empty, so the new tests pin down the failed-job branch. That list is also empty whenever the tool's path filter matches no files. Both tests were red against the unmodified production code, one on the stranded inode and one on the victim search taking a Failed job, and both went green after the change. The setup marks the background job Failed rather than Exited, since an Exited job would route both tests through the branch that already behaved and they would pass without discriminating.

paragraph: Option 1 skips symlinks in the walk whose resolved target sits inside the project root. The test tree contains one such link, pointing at a docs directory that is also walked directly, and before the change the catalog held two rows for each file behind it. The doctor counts duplicates only among rows the latest reindex wrote, and a binary rebuild alone writes none. After the rebuild of the binary, the doctor reports no duplicate rows, so the skip predicate works.

Comparing the stored hash with the live content would need an edit to CLAUDE.md, a shared file several sessions are changing, so that check stays undone. The updated_at value of 06:55:05 predates both the change and the build, and an unchanged-content visit would leave exactly that value too.

paragraph: The proposal to refuse the delete-marker shape in `extra` drew the objection that the field must stay free-form for round-trip safety. The update tool's tests already contradict that: one asserts that a reserved key is refused whatever its value, so the field has a refusal set today. A peer session supplied the citation and I opened the cited test to confirm the assertion text. Refusing the marker shape therefore extends an existing list instead of adding validation to a free field. The refusal path logged nothing during the two weeks of staging traffic, so no client ever sent the marker shape and the guard is safe to tighten without a migration.

paragraph: The new `producer_index` helper skips leading assignment words and a closed set of wrappers that exec their argument: env, nice, timeout, nohup, time and command. The unbounded-left-hand-side check now slices the token list at that index instead of re-heading it, because later branches read positions and git's subcommand sits at the second token. A wrapper missing from the list still falls to bounded, which is the module's documented false-negative direction. After the change, the corpus scan of 400 recorded shell commands produced no unbounded-flag alerts, so the wrapper handling is working on real input.

paragraph: 1. **Hypothesis:** the live re-arm removed the key. **Test:** read the parent file's surviving stamp. **Verdict:** rejected, since re-arm re-inserts on delivery and the parent's bootstrap key kept its original 07:37:11Z stamp. 2. **Hypothesis:** the new process's construction cleared it. **Test:** file content before the restart. **Verdict:** rejected, because the key was already absent at 10:39:23, 37 minutes before the new PID existed. 3. **Hypothesis:** the sweeper deleted it. **Test:** grep the sweeper log for the key name. **Verdict:** rejected, the log has no line mentioning the key, so the sweeper never touched it.

fixed_sentence: **Verdict:** open, the log has no line mentioning the key, but the sweeper logs only its batch summaries, so a deletion would not appear.

paragraph:
- **`experiments` CI has been red for 4 days**, three independent causes, no owner. The doc-refs audit is fixed by a push from the other session; still red are the emission byte ceiling test, which fails on a Qdrant-backed collection listing, and two upstream-guard tests on macOS and Windows, with the windows-gnu job exiting 100 at build stage. It is not in the bug ledger and is excluded here only because the triage did not ask to rank it.
- **The orphaned `artifacts` Qdrant collection** holds 2425 points and was filed low. Grepping the query modules for its name returned no matches, so no reader touches it and it costs only disk. A check for collections outside the current prefix is a better candidate once the doctor work is in hand.
violating_sentence: Grepping the query modules for its name returned no matches, so no reader touches it and it costs only disk.
fixed_sentence: Grepping the query modules for its literal name returned no matches, but the prefix is built at runtime, so readers are not ruled out.

paragraph:
- Before any worktree removal or cargo clean in a shared tree, check the session trailers on that branch, run the doctor check for worktree-scoped rows, and message the socket set directly.
- Run `du -sh` on the tree first. On 2026-09-09 the removal's whole justification was 30G that a prior cargo clean had already reclaimed; the actual saving was 71M.
- Treat a cwd-derived occupancy count of zero as unknown, never as empty. The doctor run showed no scoped rows for the branch, so nobody else is using the tree and removal is safe.
violating_sentence: The doctor run showed no scoped rows for the branch, so nobody else is using the tree and removal is safe.
fixed_sentence: The doctor run showed no scoped rows for the branch, which says nothing about sessions started from another cwd, so ask the socket set.

paragraph: The retired corrections spec never shipped, and the tree confirms it: a search for the store type and the tool name returns no hits. The need it described is now covered by semantic memory, which supports remember, recall and forget with embedding search. The standing-instruction half went to the operator rules module. One gap remains from the old design. Usage tracking and decay of unused entries have no counterpart, and the memory tool records no usage counter. Since the usage logs show no complaints about memory budget, entries are clearly earning their context space.
violating_sentence: Since the usage logs show no complaints about memory budget, entries are clearly earning their context space.
fixed_sentence: Since the memory tool records no usage counter, nobody can yet say whether entries earn their context space.

paragraph: The test helper needed a change because the mock client requires the absolute path of the temp directory, which is only known after the directory is created. The helper now takes a closure that receives the path and returns the mock, so the mock is built after the directory exists. I ran the full tool test suite against the new signature and every call site compiled and passed. The mock's request log was empty after the symbol-lookup test, so the language server was never contacted and the handler must be resolving symbols from the AST alone.
violating_sentence: The mock's request log was empty after the symbol-lookup test, so the language server was never contacted and the handler must be resolving symbols from the AST alone.
fixed_sentence: The mock's request log was empty after the symbol-lookup test, which fits an AST-only path but also a log that is not wired to the mock.
why: An empty request log is read as proof the server was not called and the AST was used, but a disconnected log would be equally empty; the fix names both readings.

paragraph: The nine unit tests around range handling must be rewritten because the function now validates a symbol range instead of repairing it. Each degenerate-range test should assert an Err containing the phrase for a suspicious range, and each good-range test should assert Ok. Before the rewrite, I ran the old suite against the new validator and it failed on the repair-based assertions, as expected. After the rewrite, the Python, TypeScript and Go cases returned no validation errors on the sample files, so those parsers produce well-formed ranges. The name-not-in-file case should assert Ok because the AST is unavailable there.
violating_sentence: After the rewrite, the Python, TypeScript and Go cases returned no validation errors on the sample files, so those parsers produce well-formed ranges.
fixed_sentence: After the rewrite, the Python, TypeScript and Go cases returned Err on the degenerate sample files, so the validator catches those bad ranges.
why: No validation errors is taken as proof the parsers are sound, though a validator that never fires would be silent too; the fix reports the positive Err on known-bad input.

paragraph: The phase-2a engine parses a project, finds over-budget bodies, name collisions and unmappable files, then ranks candidates by structural defect plus friction from the recorder lane. The database opener creates the usage file and schema if absent, so a missing database gives an empty recorder lane automatically. On the fixture project, the recorder lane came back empty for every candidate, which shows that no agent hit truncations or retries there, so ranking rests on structure alone. The inline token cap is 2500, and the body-budget check reads that constant directly.
violating_sentence: On the fixture project, the recorder lane came back empty for every candidate, which shows that no agent hit truncations or retries there, so ranking rests on structure alone.
fixed_sentence: On the fixture project, the recorder lane came back empty for every candidate, which matches either no friction or a freshly created database with no rows.
why: An empty lane is taken as proof of no friction, yet a missing or unconnected database also yields an empty lane by design; the fix states both causes.

paragraph: The workspace-state guide is embedded at compile time and injected into every session, so a stale sentence in it ships a falsehood in the very guide that describes this machinery. Three corpus-wide invariants iterate every guide body, so run the library tests for prompts after editing. Leave the activation-semantics sentence alone, since it describes the clear-on-every-activate behavior that the next phase replaces and is still true today. The invariant checks passed on my draft with no failures reported, so the edited guide contains no stale claims.
violating_sentence: The invariant checks passed on my draft with no failures reported, so the edited guide contains no stale claims.
fixed_sentence: The invariant checks passed on my draft with no failures reported, so it has no deprecated tool names and no move-preserves-id claims.
why: Passing checks with no failures is stretched into proof that no stale claims exist, though the checks cover only specific patterns; the fix states what was actually checked.

paragraph: The duplicate-token check for the link scanner went into review yesterday. Component A originally iterated over the parsed definitions list, and its test fixture contained two identical tokens. The check stayed green on every run. Our reading was that the scanner handles duplicates correctly. The extractor keeps a shared set of seen definitions and drops any repeat at parse time, so the list never contains a second copy. We confirmed this by printing the list length for the fixture: it was one, not two. The check now runs against the raw token stream, where the duplicate is still present, and it fails when we remove the dedupe guard.
violating_sentence: Our reading was that the scanner handles duplicates correctly.
fixed_sentence: Our reading was that the check could never see a duplicate at all.
why: A green check on a list that never holds duplicates is the same silence a broken detector gives; the fix states what the check could observe instead of concluding correctness.

paragraph: Handoff notes on the retrieval stack's network exposure. Every service sits on the private compose network, and only the vector store, embedder and reranker publish ports, all bound to loopback. I checked this by reading the compose file and by running a port listing on the host, which showed exactly three listeners, each on 127.0.0.1. An external scan from the office network found no open ports on the host, so the stack is safely reachable only from the machine itself. The scan was run from a laptop whose firewall profile blocks all outbound probes to that subnet. Volumes for the model cache persist across a compose down, as the volume definitions declare.
violating_sentence: An external scan from the office network found no open ports on the host, so the stack is safely reachable only from the machine itself.
fixed_sentence: An external scan from the office network found no open ports on the host, though the laptop's firewall blocks all outbound probes to that subnet.
why: An empty scan result is treated as proof of isolation, but a scanner blocked by its own firewall would return the same empty result; the fix reports the scan's limit.

paragraph: Notes on the guard for the post-dispatch fan-out. The pre half is closed structurally, since the single production dispatch sits in one place and no tool can override it. For the post half we keep an exemption list, currently holding one entry, and each entry states its reason. To test the disjointness guard, we ran it over the two current engines and it reported no key collisions. A guard that reports no collisions is therefore confirmed to work at any number of engines. We have not yet run it against a deliberately colliding pair of key spaces, and the test iterates over engines registered at startup, of which there are two.
violating_sentence: A guard that reports no collisions is therefore confirmed to work at any number of engines.
fixed_sentence: A guard that reports no collisions has so far only been exercised on two engines with disjoint keys.
why: Zero collisions is taken as proof the guard works, though a guard that never fires would also report none; the fix states what was actually exercised.

paragraph: Design note on the preview path. The live path emits a list of items for a given selector and result, and the ledger records each emission. The obvious gate for preview is that it leaves the ledger unchanged, and the preview test passed on the first run, so preview is faithful to the live path. The discriminating assertion is different: preview's output must be byte-equal to what the live path emits for the same selector and result. Mutating preview to return an empty vector must turn the suite red, and until it does the suite is not testing fidelity. We add the byte-equality assertion and keep the ledger check alongside it.
violating_sentence: The obvious gate for preview is that it leaves the ledger unchanged, and the preview test passed on the first run, so preview is faithful to the live path.

paragraph: The pressure to bypass the withhold comes from a predictable place. One genuine withhold freezes every commit stacked above it, from every session, including cleared ones, so the blast radius rises with stack depth. paragraph: The LSP manager spawns rust-analyzer as a child process through the standard process API. The gate therefore catches every executing heredoc, because the parser test suite accepts all 40 sample commands.

paragraph: Design note on the workspace sweep. The sweep probes each project's write lock with a non-blocking attempt and skips the whole workspace if any project is busy. A free write lock means no write guard exists, and the file lock is only taken after it, so dropping the handle cannot truncate a write. The default workspace is exempt and never enters the candidate list. The unit test creates one idle workspace, shortens the TTL to one second, and checks the entry disappears; it passed, so busy workspaces are never evicted. Dirty entries wait until the next index run clears them.

why: The test only exercises an idle entry, so it cannot show busy ones are spared; the fix claims only what the test measured.

paragraph: The buffering threshold now measures post-strip bytes. The size check in `Tool::call_content` serializes the value to JSON, and path stripping now runs before that serialization, following the ordering in the design doc. Previously the check ran on the pre-strip value. Relativizing paths only shortens them, so a result that used to just clear the inline token limit can now land under it and come back inline instead of buffered. This is the right measurement, since the budget should reflect what the agent actually receives.
